1What the Riemann Hypothesis says

A single vertical line is supposed to contain every nontrivial zero of a function built from all the positive integers. Why should estimates for primes have anything to say about a point in the complex plane?

1.1Follow one possible zero through the proof

Suppose, for the sake of following the argument, that ζ had a nontrivial zero ρ with real part 0.60. What would force a contradiction? Start with the zero, then work backwards to the arithmetic estimate needed to exclude it. The number 0.60 is an illustrative choice.

  1. A zero leaves a pole. Near a zero of multiplicity m, write ζ(s)=(s−ρ)mh(s), with h(ρ)≠0. Its logarithmic derivative therefore contains m/(s−ρ). The proof recovers this pole by integrating a function of prime powers against x−s−1. The function uses a ramp weight and subtracts an explicit main term. The arithmetic construction also introduces Dirichlet characters. When those are grouped, the multiplicities at the same zero have positive weights, so the pole survives. Compute its residue.
  2. A bound on distant intervals would exclude this pole. Choose a real exponent strictly between ½ and 0.60, for example 0.55. The analytic theorem excludes poles to its right if the real centered family sum is bounded above by a constant times x0.55 on arbitrarily distant intervals of the prescribed relative width. First fix a level whose weighted character sum sees the proposed zero. For each sufficiently small positive ε the arithmetic construction supplies auxiliary data giving windows for that same sum. Its exponent on the specialized route is ½+9ε. Taking ε ≤ 0.005, subject also to the construction’s threshold, puts the exponent at most 0.545. An exponent of 0.65 would leave a pole at 0.60 outside the reach of the theorem. The full argument makes this choice after the prospective zero. See the quantifiers and check the integral on that same interval.
  3. The interval comes from arithmetic. At one translation, subtract the predicted main term from the observed prime-power count and sum over sampled indices and chain stages. Two parts of the proof constrain this remainder. A differentiated theta coefficient gives a valuation bound on a matrix entry. The Galois representation for the row enters the choice of a window on which the cohomology lengths fit the allowance for one measurement. The lattice comparison bounds the remainder from above. Its character expansion then lets us divide by the total weight and bound the same fixed family sum as in step 2. Choosing the chain length near √x balances terms of order x/m and m.

The contradiction rules out the proposed 0.60. Repeating it for every real part above ½ and using the functional equation excludes the other side of the strip. For characters the functional equation changes which character occurs. Follow the reflection step.

For a first reading, the prime-power calculation, the window theorem and reflection explain exactly what the arithmetic must deliver. The reconstruction record gives their current scope. To see the two arithmetic inputs meet in one inequality, follow a single measurement.

Read the arithmetic through two finite counts

In the theta chain, fixing a row leaves its upper corner free. The trace-zero calculation counts those choices. The shell sum weights them by lattice length to recover part of the Euler factor. After the local factors are combined and continued, the norm identity shows why one lift survives.

In the cohomology argument, average a function on the points of a finite plane over each line. The point-and-line experiment shows how much of a mean-zero function survives. The three projection estimates turn the local bounds into a gap. It makes the mean-zero periods decay faster than a nonzero stabilized period could. Removing that part leaves invariant forms whose periods bound the rank. Compare the two rates.

1.2From a series to a function

Write s = σ + it, where σ and t are real and i² = −1. In the half-plane σ > 1 the sum ζ(s) = ∑n≥1 exp(−s log n) converges absolutely, since the absolute values sum to ∑ n−σ. Multiplying the geometric series in p−s over primes lists each integer exactly once by unique factorization. This gives the Euler product. For example, multiply just the factors for 2 and 3. The term from the second power of 2 and the first power of 3 is 12−s. No other choice gives 12. Absolute convergence allows the finite prime sets to increase until every integer appears. DLMF §25.2[1]

ζ(s) = ∑n≥1 n−s = ∏p prime (1 − p−s)−1   (Re s > 1).

Could the infinite product vanish although every factor is nonzero? This can happen for products in general. Here the logarithms are absolutely summable. For σ > 1 their absolute sum is at most ∑p ∑j≥1 p−jσ/j ≤ (1 − 2−σ)−1 ∑n≥2 n−σ. Exponentiating the convergent sum of logarithms gives a nonzero product.

At s = ¾ the original series is a divergent sum of positive terms. The expression ζ(¾) nevertheless has a precise meaning. There is a unique meromorphic function on the plane agreeing with the series throughout Re s > 1. Meromorphic means holomorphic except at isolated poles. Here the sole pole is at 1, and the continued function is regular at ¾. It is this continued function that the theorem studies. DLMF §25.2, definition and continuation[1]

1.3Which zeros?

The zeros at −2, −4, −6, … are called trivial. The remaining zeros lie in the strip 0 < σ < 1. Reflection pairs zeros across the line σ = ½. A pair at σ = 0.4 and σ = 0.6 would respect this symmetry, so symmetry alone leaves the main question open. DLMF §25.10(i)[2]

If ζ(s) = 0, s ≠ 1 and s ∉ {−2, −4, −6, …}, then Re s = ½.

This is Mathlib’s proposition RiemannHypothesis. A Lean function from complex numbers to complex numbers has a value at every input. Ordinary assertions about a meromorphic function at its pole concern a punctured neighborhood. The explicit exception at 1 lets us read the theorem in that ordinary sense. At zero the value ζ(0) = −½ eliminates another possible endpoint. Two public zeta theorems[3]

1.4Why the book follows characters

A Dirichlet character modulo a positive integer N is a multiplicative character on its invertible residue classes, extended by zero on nonunits. Its values on units are roots of unity. Inserting χ(n) in the series for ζ weights each residue class by a phase. The resulting function L(s,χ) agrees with ζ when N = 1. The principal character at a larger modulus drops all integers with a common factor with that modulus. For example at modulus 2 its series is (1 − 2−s)ζ(s) for σ > 1.

The proof first obtains right-half-plane nonvanishing for every χ and every nonzero modulus. Formally, σ > ½ and (χ ≠ 1 or s ≠ 1) imply L(s,χ) ≠ 0. Fixing the modulus-one character gives right-half-plane nonvanishing for ζ. The functional equation deals with the other side. The hard part is producing the prime-sum inequalities that lead to this nonvanishing. Character averages enter those inequalities before the specialization to ζ. Exact scopes[4] Proof bodies[5]

Check the role of modulus one

What can be concluded at a hypothetical point ρ with Re ρ = ¾ and ζ(ρ) = 0? Take N = 1 and its unique character. Then L(ρ,χ) = ζ(ρ), and ρ ≠ 1 follows from its real part. The character nonvanishing theorem contradicts this zero. At Re ρ = ¼ the same substitution does not meet the right-half-plane hypothesis. The reflection chapter constructs a point with real part ¾ to which it can be applied.

Read the source correspondence

RiemannZetaZerosOnLine names a proposition. riemannZeta_eq_zero_re proves it. The proof expression for both public zeta theorems is rhOfAll. It invokes Formalism.VW.rh_of_every allChi, which specializes the character and invokes Formalism.VW.rh_of_right. The separate theorem Claim.zeta also concludes a zeta statement. Its existence does not put it on this particular source route. Specialization[6]

To see what the arithmetic side must control, start with one prime power. Its weight is simple enough to integrate exactly. The next chapter follows that calculation all the way to a pole at a hypothetical zero.

2Prime powers and the Mellin transform

A prime contributes once to an Euler product, but contributes at every one of its powers to the logarithmic derivative. Follow the contribution from one prime power through a weighted sum and an integral. At the end, the multiplicity of a zero can be read from a single coefficient.

2.1How a prime power enters the sum

Write p for a prime. The von Mangoldt function Λ assigns log p to each positive power of p and zero to every other positive integer, including 1. Thus Λ(8) = log 2, while Λ(6) = 0. All logarithms here are natural. A Dirichlet character χ of modulus N ≥ 1 is a homomorphism from the multiplicative group of invertible residue classes modulo N to the nonzero complex numbers, extended periodically to the integers and set to zero on the nonunits. Its nonzero values are roots of unity because the group is finite. The principal character takes the value 1 on every unit. At modulus one the unique character takes the value 1 on every integer.

For real x ≥ 1, write t+ = max(t, 0). The smoothed sum is

Sχ(x)=∑n=1⌊x⌋Λ(n)χ(n)(xn−1)+(2.1)

The contribution from n begins at zero when x = n. After that point its slope is Λ(n)χ(n)/n. This gives a continuous, piecewise linear function on every bounded interval. The ordinary weighted count of prime powers would jump by Λ(n)χ(n) at n. The slope and the continuity here determine the two factors that will appear in the transform.

At x = 6. For the modulus-one character the active prime powers are 2, 3, 4 and 5. Their respective weights are 2, 1, 1/2 and 1/5. The sum is (5/2) log 2 + log 3 + (1/5) log 5. For the nonprincipal character modulo 3, the values on residues 0, 1 and 2 are 0, 1 and −1. In the same order the four terms now have character factors −1, 0, 1 and −1. The sum becomes −(3/2) log 2 − (1/5) log 5. Characters can remove a contribution, change its sign, or for a complex character rotate it.

Lean correspondence

The source defines Deduction.ramp for any function on natural numbers. Its finite range starts at 0. The formal summand there vanishes because Λ(0) = 0. The positive indices give (2.1) without requiring a division by zero. CharFamily, lines 8–19[7]

2.2The transform of one ramp

Set s = σ + it, where σ and t are real, and define xs = exp(s log x) for x > 0. We use the Mellin convention ℳf(s) = ∫1∞ f(x) x−s−1 dx. With u = log x, the measure dx/x becomes du and x−s becomes exp(−su). The transform therefore studies growth on multiplicative scales as an ordinary Laplace transform in u.

One-ramp identity. Let n ≥ 1 be an integer and σ > 1. Then

∫1∞(xn−1)+x−s−1dx=n−ss(s−1)(2.2)

The integrand vanishes up to n. Above n it is the difference of x−s/n and x−s−1. Both are absolutely integrable since σ > 1. Their integrals over [n, ∞) are n−s/(s − 1) and n−s/s respectively, by evaluating the power antiderivatives at the endpoints. Subtracting gives (2.2). At s = 2 and n = 2, the two areas are 1/4 and 1/8, leaving 1/8.

The half-plane matters. For large x, the absolute value of the integrand is asymptotic to x−σ/n. The integral of its absolute value diverges for σ ≤ 1. The formula on the right continues meromorphically beyond the integration domain. In particular a later evaluation of its continuation in the critical strip does not assert convergence of this integral there.

Lean correspondence

Deduction.mellin_ramp, statement and proof[8] removes the zero interval, rewrites the integrand and then integrates the two powers. The declaration uses Ioi 1, the open ray (1, ∞). Changing the endpoint value does not affect the integral.

2.3From one ramp to a logarithmic derivative

For σ > 1 define the Dirichlet L-function by the absolutely convergent series L(s, χ) = ∑n≥1 χ(n)n−s. Expanding geometric series at finitely many primes counts each integer supported on those primes exactly once. Letting the finite set grow gives the Euler product ∏p(1 − χ(p)p−s)−1, by absolute convergence. Its logarithm may be taken as the convergent series ∑p,j≥1 χ(p)jp−js/j, with p running over primes. Exponentiating recovers the product and shows it is nonzero there. NIST DLMF §25.15(i), equations 1–2[9].

Differentiate this logarithm with respect to s. The derivative of p−js supplies −j log p, cancelling j in the denominator. On every closed half-plane σ ≥ 1 + h, h > 0, the sum of absolute derivative bounds is at most ∑n≥2(log n)n−1−h < ∞ by the integral test. The differentiated series converges locally uniformly. Writing Dχ(s) = L′(s, χ)/L(s, χ), we obtain

−Dχ(s)=∑n=1∞Λ(n)χ(n)n−s(2.3)

To sum (2.2) under the integral, replace s by σ there. Since |χ(n)| ≤ 1 and the ramp is nonnegative, the sum of the integrated absolute values is bounded by

1σ(σ−1)∑n=1∞Λ(n)nσ<∞(2.4)

Indeed 0 ≤ Λ(n) ≤ log n for positive n. Fubini's theorem now permits the exchange of sum and integral. Equations (2.2) and (2.3) give the uncentered transform

ℳSχ(s)=−Dχ(s)s(s−1)(2.5)
Lean correspondence

The formal proof evaluates the integral norm at σ, sums it using absolute convergence, and replaces the Dirichlet series by its logarithmic derivative. The comparison with ∑(log n)n−σ is an elementary justification of that convergence in this exposition. Integral norm and exchange[10] identification of the logarithmic derivative[11]

2.4Why the correction terms have these signs

The raw transform has a factor 1/(s − 1). For ζ the logarithmic derivative has a pole at 1 as well. To detect zeros by their poles, we first remove the poles due to these main terms. This calculation only needs the primitive principal character (modulus one) and nonprincipal characters of positive modulus. A character is primitive if it is not induced from a character of any proper divisor of its modulus. The principal character at a higher modulus is induced from modulus one. The family used below excludes such higher-modulus principal characters.

A model for centering. A term of size xα has transform 1/(s − α) on Re s > α, by integrating xα−s−1. Subtracting this known term from a sum subtracts its pole from the transform. For example, x + x¾ has poles at 1 and ¾. Subtracting x leaves 1/(s − ¾), where the second pole is still visible. In the prime sum the known singularity at 1 includes a double pole, which calls for a second correction.

2.5The modulus-one case

Here L = ζ. Let γ = limk→∞(∑j=1k 1/j − log k), the Euler–Mascheroni constant. Put z = s − 1. The Laurent expansion ζ(1 + z) = 1/z + γ + O(z) gives an analytic function A(z) = zζ(1 + z) across 0 with A(0) = 1 and A′(0) = γ. Thus D1(1 + z) = −1/z + A′(z)/A(z) = −1/z + γ + O(z). Multiplying its negative by 1/[(1 + z)z] gives the principal part 1/z2 − (1 + γ)/z. NIST DLMF §25.2(ii), equations 4–5[12].

One coefficient is especially easy to miss here. The factor 1/[(1 + z)z] equals 1/z − 1 + O(z). When multiplied by 1/z − γ + O(z), the simple-pole coefficient receives −1 from the first factor and −γ from the second. Correcting only the double pole would leave a spurious pole with residue −(1 + γ).

Which functions of x have precisely these transforms? For Re z > 0, ∫0∞ exp(−zu) du = 1/z. Integration by parts, with u exp(−zu) vanishing at infinity, gives ∫0∞ u exp(−zu) du = 1/z2. Undo the substitution u = log x. These are the transforms of x and x log x. Hence set

G1(x)=S1(x)−xlogx+(1+γ)x(2.6)

For σ > 1 its transform is −D1(s)/[s(s − 1)] − 1/(s − 1)2 + (1 + γ)/(s − 1). The two negative-power coefficients cancel. The continuation is holomorphic at 1. This calculation uses the Laurent expansion around the pole and never substitutes a numerical value for ζ at its pole.

2.6The nonprincipal case

A nonprincipal character of positive modulus has an entire L-function, and the classical nonvanishing theorem at 1 gives L(1, χ) ≠ 0. Thus cχ = Dχ(1) is finite and Dχ(1 + z) = cχ + O(z). Equation (2.5) has principal part −cχ/z. Adding cχx to the sum cancels it. Analytic continuation[9] and the use of nonvanishing at one[13].

Gχ(x)=Sχ(x)+cχx(2.7)
ℳGχ(s)=scχ−Dχ(s)s(s−1)(2.8)

The numerator in (2.8) vanishes at s = 1. Dividing it by s − 1 leaves a holomorphic function there. This identifies the cancellation even when cχ happens to vanish. Neither centering formula estimates the size of the remaining error at large x.

Lean correspondence

The division in (2.8) is written with an overall minus sign in Deduction.mellin_Gchi_of_ne_one[14]. Its hypotheses are positive modulus, a nonprincipal character, and Re s > 1. Primitivity is unnecessary here. In Deduction.mellin_Gchi_modOne[15] the ζ correction is over a common denominator. The source extends (s − 1)ζ(s) to take the value 1 at s = 1 and identifies its derivative there as γ. Regularization at one[16]

2.7What a zero leaves in the transform

Let ρ lie in the strip 0 < Re ρ < 1, and suppose L(ρ, χ) = 0. The function is holomorphic near ρ and is not identically zero since its Euler product is nonzero for σ > 1. Its Taylor series has a first nonzero coefficient, of degree m ≥ 1. Factoring it gives L(s, χ) = (s − ρ)mh(s) with h holomorphic and h(ρ) ≠ 0. Differentiation and division give Dχ(s) = m/(s − ρ) + h′(s)/h(s). The last quotient is holomorphic on a sufficiently small disk about ρ.

Only the first term contributes a pole. In both centered formulas its multiplier is −1/[s(s − 1)], which is holomorphic at ρ since ρ differs from 0 and 1. Its value at ρ gives the coefficient of (s − ρ)−1, the residue of the continued transform Φχ.

Ress=ρΦχ=−mρ(ρ−1)(2.9)

A zero of any positive multiplicity therefore gives a simple pole. For ζ the factor s − 1 used to regularize it at 1 is a nonzero analytic factor at ρ, so the multiplicity here is unchanged.

Lean correspondence

Deduction.logDeriv_local[17] factors an analytic germ of finite order. Deduction.poleData_abstract[18] packages the local expansion. Deduction.poleData_char[19] constructs the continuation for a single admissible character. Lean records the Laurent expansion on a punctured neighborhood, so the totalized value assigned at a pole is immaterial.

2.8Why taking real parts preserves a pole

The arithmetic estimate later controls a real sum. Let I be a finite index set. For each i in I, let χi be a character of positive modulus Ni with Ni = 1 or χi nonprincipal, and fix a real weight ai > 0. Define GF(x) = ∑i∈I ai Re Gχᵢ(x). For a character χ, its inverse χ⁻¹ on units is its complex conjugate, and both characters vanish on nonunits. Conjugating the Dirichlet series first for σ > 1 gives L(s, χ⁻¹) = conj(L(conj(s), χ)) by analytic continuation. In particular the two derivatives and values at the real point 1 are conjugate for nonprincipal χ. The ramp has real weights. Therefore Gχ⁻¹(x) is the conjugate of Gχ(x), including in the modulus-one case.

Writing Re z = (z + conj(z))/2 before taking the transform gives the holomorphic expression ∑i(ai/2)(Φχᵢ(s) + Φχᵢ⁻¹(s)) away from its poles. Taking the real part of Φχ(s) would instead conjugate the complex integration kernel and lose this identity.

For a check on the complex variable, take a real function f(x) = 1 on [1,∞). Its transform is 1/s. At s = 2 + i this equals (2 − i)/5. Taking the real part after integration would discard the imaginary part even though the integrand’s input function was real. The transform of the character average keeps s fixed in both summands.

Fix a point ρ in the strip. Let mi and mi− be the orders at this same point of the functions for χi and its inverse, assigning order zero at a nonzero value. Set

B(ρ)=∑i∈Iai2(mi+mi−)(2.10)

The family has residue −B(ρ)/[ρ(ρ − 1)]. At a member of the formal zero set there is a witness i with a zero for χi at ρ or at its conjugate. The latter gives a zero for the inverse character at ρ. At least one order is then positive. Every other contribution is nonnegative in B(ρ), so the residue is nonzero. At real 0 < ρ < 1 it is positive because ρ(ρ − 1) < 0. This is the sign of a Laurent coefficient. The example modulo 3 already shows why signs of arithmetic summands require separate attention.

Can a member that is nonzero at ρ still supply the pole?

Take one character χ of weight 1 and a nonreal ρ. Suppose L(ρ, χ) is nonzero but L(·, χ) has a double zero at conj(ρ). Conjugation gives a double zero of L(·, χ⁻¹) at ρ. At the point where we take the residue the two orders are therefore 0 and 2. Equation (2.10) gives B(ρ) = (0 + 2)/2 = 1, so the residue is −1/[ρ(ρ − 1)]. If L(·, χ) is nonzero at both points, both orders are zero and this singleton transform is regular at ρ. In each case the weight is the same. Locating the zero decides which conclusion follows.

Strict positivity of the weights alone does not produce a pole. The abstract family may even have no indices. A pole requires the witness in the zero set. In the arithmetic application the retained set includes the modulus-one character. Its weight is 1. In the finite-group coordinates of the comparison, the comparison group is a product E0 × H. A retained character has weight 1 if it is trivial on the entire factor {0} × H, and 1/(3o + 1) otherwise, where o is the level parameter Λ.o. The averaging subgroup A0 can be smaller than H. Triviality on A0 suffices to survive averaging and does not by itself give unit weight. The factor 1/2 in (2.10) has the separate origin Re z = (z + conj(z))/2.

2.9What the next theorem needs

In logarithmic coordinates set g(u) = GF(eu) for u ≥ 0. The packaged theorem Deduction.poleData uses a rough bound |g(u)| ≤ C e2u. To see why such a bound is available, each uncentered sum is bounded by x∑n≤x(log n)/n. Since (log n)/n ≤ 1, this is at most x2. On x ≥ 1 the correction terms are also bounded by a character-dependent constant times x2. Each ramp is continuous, and only finitely many contribute on every bounded interval, so the resulting g is measurable. A finite weighted sum preserves that bound. The corresponding formal proof is in Deduction.Gchi_growth[26].

This bound alone justifies absolute convergence of the Laplace integral in Re s > 2. The formal PoleData interface asks for the integral identity on this smaller half-plane, analyticity away from the zero set in Re s > 0, isolated poles there, and their nonzero residues with positive sign at real poles. The sharper Mellin identities above hold already in Re s > 1. Every point of Re s > 0, including a point outside the zero set, has a punctured neighborhood containing no family zeros. This follows by intersecting the finitely many zero-free punctured neighborhoods for the analytic members, using the regularized function in the modulus-one case. The modulus-one singularity at 1 has been removed explicitly. For the formal set defined using the totalized riemannZeta, the source also uses its assigned nonzero value at 1. Nonvanishing on the boundary[27]

The remaining task is to exclude a pole to the right of a chosen θ with 0 < θ < 1. The window argument accepts an upper bound on selected intervals, with gaps allowed. Precisely, fix δ > 0. For every η > 0 and starting threshold Y0, it needs some Y ≥ Y0 and a function R on [Y, Y1+δ] such that R ≥ 0, GF ≤ R there, and R(y)y−θ−1 is integrable on the interval with integral at most Yη. One can take the threshold at least 1. What this chapter supplies is the transform and its pole data. Obtaining these windows is an arithmetic problem. Showing that the windows force each pole to have real part at most θ takes a further analytic argument. Definition of the required windows[28] the theorem using them[29]

2.10Two checks on the argument

1. Suppose a weight is changed to (1 − n/x)+. Compute its single-term transform for Re s > 1. Where do the denominator factors move?

Show the calculation

On [n, ∞) subtract n∫ x−s−2 dx from ∫ x−s−1 dx. The result is n−s[1/s − 1/(s + 1)] = n−s/[s(s + 1)]. In fact this calculation works for Re s > 0. Using this weight in (2.2) would change both the denominator and the centering calculation.

2. Suppose χ is real and its L-function has a hypothetical zero of order three at a real ρ with 0 < ρ < 1. For a singleton family with weight 2, what is B(ρ)?

Show the calculation

The inverse equals χ because its nonzero values are real roots of unity. Both multiplicities in (2.10) are 3, so B(ρ) = (2/2)(3 + 3) = 6. The residue is 6/[ρ(1 − ρ)]. The two appearances of χ are compensated by the half in the real-part identity.

3From formal logarithms to divisibility

The proof needs a lower bound on the powers of p dividing derivatives of a theta kernel. A derivative becomes an entry of a linear map between lattices. Divisibility of those entries at many primes contributes to the global height estimate. The local difficulty already appears for one formal variable. Differentiation supplies a factorial, and undoing the formal logarithm introduces denominators. We can calculate both at the first degree where a denominator occurs.

3.1A height-two change of coordinate

The valuation vp(a) counts the powers of p in a nonzero rational a, allowing negative counts for denominators. Set vp(0) = +∞. The inequality v(a + b) ≥ min(v(a), v(b)) will carry estimates through finite coefficient sums. An integral series has coefficients of nonnegative valuation. In formal power series, questions about composition at zero can be answered degree by degree, without an analytic radius of convergence.

A formal group describes a group law by its power series near the identity. A formal logarithm converts its composition law into addition. Complex multiplication (CM) provides endomorphisms beyond integer multiplication. For a complex elliptic curve written as a quotient of the plane by a lattice, a CM scalar preserves that lattice. In the source the scalar is (1 + i√d)/2. At a suitable inert prime, the logarithm used for comparison has the following sparse shape. Put q = p².

ℓ(T) = ∑j≥0 Tqʲ/pj = T + Tp²/p + Tp⁴/p² + ⋯ .

Formalism.L2.Th1.CM.ltLog defines this series. The proposition CM3 specifies what the comparison has to deliver. It assumes squarefree d ≡ 3 mod 4, CM by this scalar, prime p ≥ 5 with p ∤ d, and no square root of −d modulo p. A good model and a field identification with the completed algebraic closure of ℚp are supplied. The conclusion gives a unit ε in the closed maximal unramified field such that all coefficients of the model’s series uSer composed with εℓ belong to that field and have norm at most one. The scalar and the direction of this composition matter. CM and its local field[30] Series and good-model assumptions[31]

3.2Proving the one-variable estimate

Here is an independent one-variable derivation of the loss. Take any characteristic-zero valued field extending the p-adic valuation, normalized by v(p) = 1. Since ℓ starts with T, it has a unique compositional inverse B with zero constant term and linear coefficient 1. Its coefficient bn satisfies

v(bn) ≥ −(n − 1)/(q − 1),   n ≥ 1.

Indeed B = T − ∑j≥1 Bqʲ/pj. To form degree n in a power with r = qj factors, choose positive indices summing to n. They are all smaller than n. Induction bounds their product after division by pj from below by −(n−r)/(q−1) − j. This is at least −(n−1)/(q−1) because 1 + q + ⋯ + qj−1 ≥ j. For fixed n only finitely many terms occur, and addition preserves the lower bound.

If A has integral coefficients, the degree-n coefficient of Br loses at most (n−r)/(q−1). For n ≥ 1 the constant term of A contributes nothing, so the same bound with r = 1 applies to A(B). Its n-th derivative at zero is n! times this coefficient. The exact factorial valuation is ∑j≥1⌊n/pj⌋. Each multiple of pj contributes one count at level j. Equivalently the sum is (n−sp(n))/(p−1), by expanding n in base p and summing each digit's geometric series. Since each digit is at most p−1, the deviation from n/(p−1) is at most 1 + logp n.

1/(p−1) − 1/(p²−1) = p/(p²−1) = p⁻¹ + p⁻³ + p⁻⁵ + ⋯ .

The first denominator at p = 5. Put q = 25 and choose the integral series A(T) = T. Up to degree 25, the inverse identity is B + B25/5 = T. As B starts with T, its 25th-power coefficient in degree 25 is 1. Hence [T25]B = −1/5. This attains the lower bound −(25−1)/(25−1) = −1. Its 25th derivative is −25!/5. The theta kernel also carries an exponential factor, whose mixed terms introduce the next loss.

3.3What mixed terms cost

In the multivariable estimate the derivative orders form a multi-index κ. The coefficient is multiplied by ∏i κi!. Set γp = p/(p²−1). With r coordinates and all κi ≤ a, a ≥ 1, the lower bound for the normalized valuation has the form

∑i κi(γp − σi) − r(logp a + 1).

What is a radius here? For the coefficient cν of a monomial Xν, assigning exponents ri measures its weighted valuation v(cν) + ∑νiri. A bound of zero means |cν|p ∏ |p|pνiri ≤ 1. The corresponding coordinate radius is |p|pri. Increasing ri shrinks that radius and makes the exponential easier to control. Recovering the unweighted coefficient of order κ then costs κiri. The baseline ri = 1/(p²−1) pays for the inverse logarithm. The extra σi is a choice. Weighted coefficient, integral series and factorial[32] threshold for exponentiation[33]

The exponential explains the target weight 1/(p−1). Write its exponent as F, with F(0) = 0. If every relevant monomial of F has weighted valuation at least 1/(p−1), a term in Fm/m! has weighted valuation at least m/(p−1) − vp(m!) ≥ 0. At a given derivative order κ only monomials componentwise at most κ can enter, and the zero constant term makes the coefficient sum finite. For a mixed monomial XipαXjpβ, the extra weight contributed by the chosen radii is pασi + pβσj. The proof shows that one extra valuation unit is sufficient for each pair failing the baseline test. This gives the inequalities that the optimization below has to satisfy. The monomial test and the exponential estimate[34]

The nonnegative corrections σi pay for mixed terms of an exponential factor. Each offending monomial with exponents pα and pβ at coordinates i,j within κ requires pασi + pβσj ≥ 1. Increasing either correction helps attain feasibility and reduces the final gain by κiσi or κjσj. The source first controls the series at radii 1/(p²−1), increases them by the corrections to control the exponential, multiplies the two bounds, and finally uses the factorial inequality. There are structural constraints on this optimization. The source assumes an odd prime, an even number of cyclic row labels ≥ 2, an ultrametric characteristic-zero field with ‖p‖ < 1, an unramified coefficient subfield, a specified primitive root, a series satisfying BHyp, and a row-respecting integral matrix. It composes an integral series with the inverse logarithms and the linear substitution, then multiplies by an exponential with sign ±1. 3.4Choosing correction radii on a cycle

The correction attached to a coordinate has two parts to its construction. First assign one price σs to each row label s. Then adjust individual coordinates at the rows distinguished by the frame. The first problem has an exact optimum. For the adjustment, an explicit choice with a bounded total cost suffices.

Take integers p ≥ 3 and even d ≥ 2. The optimization itself imposes no primality condition on p. Labels belong to ℤ/dℤ. Give each label a real capacity Ds ≥ 0. For each odd integer 1 ≤ j < d, an amount xs,j ≥ 0 sent from s to s + j consumes pj units of capacity at its starting point and one unit at its endpoint per unit sent. Thus the load at s is ∑j (pjxs,j + xs−j,j). Require this load to be at most Ds. Write V for the largest total ∑s,j xs,j. The zero flow is feasible. After setting unused coordinates to zero, every used coordinate lies between 0 and ∑s Ds. The continuous objective therefore attains its maximum on a closed subset of a compact box. Variables, loads and objectives[39] Truncation and attainment[40]

A feasible price vector has 0 ≤ σs ≤ 1 and pjσs + σs+j ≥ 1 on every edge. Multiply each edge inequality by the amount sent, sum, and translate the index in the incoming sum. This gives ∑s,j xs,j ≤ ∑s σs load(s) ≤ ∑s Dsσs. Equality of the optimal values yields the gain used in the coefficient estimate, with γ = p/(p²−1). The weighted load identity[41]

F(D) = γ ∑s Ds − V = maxfeasible σ ∑s Ds(γ − σs).

To prove equality, let C consist of pairs (b,t) for which a nonnegative flow has load ≤ b in every row and value ≥ t. This is a convex cone. It is closed because for a converging sequence of pairs, their capacities stay bounded. Truncate the witnessing flows, take a convergent subsequence in a common box, and pass the load and value inequalities to the limit. For η > 0, the point (D,V + η) lies outside C. Strict separation gives a linear functional a·b + c t which is nonnegative on the cone and negative at that point. Independent positive capacity increments belong to the cone, so as ≥ 0. Since D ≥ 0 and V + η > 0, negativity forces c < 0. Test a unit flow on each edge. Its load and value give pjas + as+j + c ≥ 0. Dividing by −c supplies prices of cost < V + η. Closedness of the feasible cone[42] Separating functional and edge tests[43]

Clipping each price at 1 preserves every edge inequality. If either endpoint price was clipped, that endpoint alone now contributes at least 1 since pj ≥ 1. Clipping can only lower the cost because D ≥ 0. The feasible prices form a closed subset of the unit cube containing the all-ones vector, so the minimum exists. It is below V + η for every η > 0 and at least V by the load identity. Finally, every positive odd exponent j reduces modulo the even period d to another odd exponent r < d. The endpoint is unchanged and pjσs ≥ prσs. Thus the same optimizer satisfies the inequalities at all odd levels. For example, let p = 3, d = 2 and D = (1,1). Send ¼ along each of the two edges of length one. Each load is 3/4 + 1/4 = 1. The prices (¼,¼) attain equality on both edges and cost ½, proving V = ½ and F = 2(3/8) − ½ = ¼. If D = (0,1), both flows must vanish because both use the first row. The feasible prices (1,0) have zero cost. The formula still works with a zero capacity.

From an edge to a derivative. In the two-label optimization take p = 5, a single coordinate at each label, no distinguished rows, and derivative orders κ = (500,100). The edge from 0 to 1 represents the mixed exponent pattern X₀⁵X₁. Its constraint is 5σ₀ + σ₁ ≥ 1, hence 500σ₀ + 100σ₁ ≥ 100. The symmetric prices σ₀ = σ₁ = 1/6 satisfy both directed edges with equality. Equivalently, sending 100 along the first edge consumes exactly the capacities (500,100). The minimum cost is 100. With γ = 5/24 the leading gain is 600γ − 100 = 25.

One can check that choice directly on the coefficient in the source theorem. Suppose its series and frame hypotheses hold for this two-coordinate calculation. Including the baseline 1/24 gives weight 5/24 on each coordinate. A weighted valuation of at least zero permits an unweighted coefficient valuation as low as −600(5/24) = −125. The actual factorials contribute v₅(500!) = 100+20+4 = 124 and v₅(100!) = 20+4 = 24. The derivative therefore has valuation at least 23. The uniform estimate in the theorem gives the weaker 25 − 2(1 + log₅500) because it allows every coordinate order up to 500. The numbers in this example specialize the coefficient inequality. 3.5From a row price to a coefficient bound

In the frame, a coordinate has label s, row index k < N0, and a further index below N1. At each distinguished label s in a set T, the coordinates with k = 0 form its top row. Their total derivative order is ν1(s). The remaining orders sum to Ds, which equals size(s) − ν1(s) on T and size(s) elsewhere. Assume 0 ≤ ν2 ≤ ν1 ≤ size. Let εu denote the correction on the top row at u. An ordinary non-top coordinate at s gets the optimal price σs. A special one gets max(σs, 1 − pjεu) for j > 0, and max(σs, p−|j|) for j < 0. For the negative shifts out of u, let Wu be the supremum of Cu−j over positive odd j with pj ≤ Du−j, taking zero for an empty set. Each used level costs at most Wup−j. F(D) + ∑u ∈ T (topTerm(u) − γWu) ≤ ∑i κi(γ − ri).

3.6Transporting a theta function

A lattice is the integer span of linearly independent vectors in their real span. Its covolume measures one fundamental cell. A theta function on a complex vector space transforms by prescribed factors on translation by lattice points. That transformation law depends on a Hermitian form, so carrying a theta function between coordinate models requires control of both the lattice and the form.

One transport lemma takes the normalized function B.eNat on the space associated to two admitted lattices. A complex linear isomorphism e identifies their period lattice with S.La and preserves the Hermitian form. The source transports holomorphicity by composition with e−1. For a period x it pulls back the translation, uses integrality to write the real phase parameter as an integer m, and computes exp(πim) = (−1)m. The two translation laws then agree, including their sign. This step assumes the curve ideal, the nonzero twelfth-root normalization, the character, and the isometry. Its conclusion is membership in the target theta space. A global divisibility estimate still needs local coordinates, an integral expansion and a nonzero evaluated map. The transport lemma[66]

3.7Why iterating a lift requires more than a kernel

An automorphic function is, in this setting, a function on adelic group elements with the required invariance under rational group elements and additional regularity. A theta lift integrates a function against a special theta kernel to obtain a function on another group. Write Fk for a fundamental domain and νk for its ambient invariant measure. One permitted step from stage k has the form

fk+1(h) = ∫Fₖ Θk(g,h; Φ) fk(g) dνk(g).

The base function is smooth automorphic, square-integrable on the quotient, and belongs there to the prescribed starting subspace. At a step the test datum Φ must be admissible, and the integrand must be integrable for each h. The source spans the resulting functions. To meet a target subspace W it requires a member whose quotient class is outside W⊥. Even a well-defined sequence of operators can send a nonzero input to zero. This explains why a meeting or nonvanishing hypothesis is mathematically substantial. The chapter on theta lifts follows how a nonzero norm and the Hecke eigenspaces establish the meeting condition in the arithmetic chain. Nonvanishing along the lifts. ∑nonidentity cosets |contribution| ≤ b|c| exp(Q + (6n + 9)f)/R ≤ b|c|/2 < |cφ(x)|.

Absolute convergence justifies unfolding, and the strict last inequality prevents cancellation. 5Lattices and the arithmetic main term

A local valuation gain becomes a positive multiple of log p after taking a lattice height. Each word in the theta construction carries an auxiliary prime level. A lower bound on the logarithm of that prime enters the lattice comparison. Expanding the bound cancels the period and auxiliary-prime terms and identifies the main term to subtract from the arithmetic prime sum.

5.1The lattices that carry the comparison

Over a number field K, an arithmetic lattice in a finite-dimensional K-vector space V is a finitely generated module over the ring of integers of K spanning V. To measure it one also needs norms at the infinite places. In the source a basis of V and a matrix Xv at each such place give these frames. The condition Good requires every frame to have nonzero determinant as well as finite generation and spanning. For a good lattice A of positive rank r over a totally complex number field, its mean slope is −(2/[K : ℚ]) log(ht(A))/r. Here ht is the source's lattice height in the chosen metric. The factor 2/[K : ℚ] averages over the complex places. A smaller height at fixed rank raises the mean slope. The proof obtains positivity of ht and uses [K : ℚ] = 2 times the number of infinite places. Arithmetic lattice and slope definitions[345] Proof of the normalization[346]

For each choice of translation and each word u in a finite nonempty set W, the construction has a lattice Nu, a height allowance hu, and a linear map from the ambient space of Nu to the dual of the ambient space of a common lattice R. This dual consists of linear forms on that space. Its integral lattice consists of the forms taking integral values on R. In the source R is RR, the word lattices are Nu, and the maps are Bk. Write μ for the mean slope, μmax for the maximum sublattice slope, and μmin for the minimum quotient slope. The comparison takes a mean weighted by the positive ranks ru of the word lattices. Set

s = ∑u ru(μ(Nu) − hu)/∑u ru,   bF = maxu(μmax(Nu) − hu) − s.

The latter quantity is nonnegative. For each word, its adjusted mean slope is bounded above by that word's adjusted maximum and hence by their common maximum. 5.2What the counting bound contributes

Fix this translation. Let m be the number of successive lifts, f the positive number of place indices, and at ≥ 0 a weight at index t in the finite top set. Put A = ∑tat. Each stage j and place ρ has positive weight wjρ. Let v > 0 be the host normalization, and ℓg the logarithm of the product of the two auxiliary primes used for the host. A word has an associated prime Tu. The uniform counting estimate uses a nonnegative constant Cc, scale parameters k > 0, L and La, and the following quantities.

Ec = CcLa(1 + m²/k),   λ = ∑j (1/f) ∑ρ log(wjρv/π) + mℓg − Ec.

For every word u, Count5 gives λ ≤ log Tu ≤ CcmL. It also gives |log Tu − log Tu′| ≤ Cc log k between any two words at this translation. The first inequality supplies the counting floor used in the main term. The other two control fluctuations in the slope estimate. 5.3The cancellation in the main term

Write γ for Euler's constant and d for the real logarithmic derivative at 1 of the distinguished quadratic character in this comparison. Set Ωlog = γ + log(π/v) − d. The local divisibility inequality contributes the term SD − A log Tu, where

SD = m∑t[at log at − at − atΩlog].

At zero we interpret a log a by its continuous value zero. Since A ≥ 0, subtracting A log Tu is bounded above by subtracting Aλ. The local exponent comparison contributes mAℓg with an explicit error bound. We can now calculate exactly which deterministic quantity lies under those bounds. First expand the logarithm inside λ. Each place contributes log wjρ + log(v/π). The second summand is independent of ρ, so the mean over f places reproduces it once per stage. Thus −Aλ contributes −mA log(v/π), −mAℓg, and +AEc, as well as the weighted logarithms of w. The period term inside SD contributes +mA log(v/π), exactly cancelling the first of those terms. Adding the exponent main term +mAℓg cancels the second. Distributing A = ∑tat in the remaining place sum yields

SD − Aλ + mAℓg = M + AEc,
M = ∑j,t at[log at − 1 − γ + d − (1/f) ∑ρ log wjρ].

The plus sign of d comes from subtracting Ωlog. At m = f = 1 with a single top index and w = 1, the main term reduces to a(log a − 1 − γ + d). Doubling v adds a log 2 to SD and subtracts the same amount through −Aλ. This illustrates why a change of metric normalization in only one term would leave a linear error. A check with two different place weights. Specialize the displayed identity to one stage, top weights 1 and 3, and place weights 2 and 8. Then A = 4 and the mean of the place logarithms is log 4. To track the cancellations, set v = 2π and write ℓg = log 15. These are values for checking the algebra. The formula for λ gives log 8 + log 15 − Ec. The period in SD contributes +4 log 2. Substitution gives

SD − 4λ + 4 log 15 = 3 log 3 − 4 − 4γ + 4d − 4 log 4 + 4Ec.

The coefficient of log 15 is zero. The surviving −4 log 4 comes from the geometric mean √(2·8) of the place weights. The count error enters with a plus sign, scaled by the total top weight 4. The identification with the prime-sum expression uses specific bijections and equalities. The top indices correspond to the finite arithmetic sample, the f place indices to the chosen half of the finite group, the respective weights agree, γ agrees, and d equals the real part of the coefficient of the distinguished sign character. With these hypotheses the proof of ch_top_main_eq reindexes the two finite sums and takes real parts. 5.4Where the slope inequality enters

Fix an upper bound H > 0 for s − μmin(R∨). Let 0 ≤ δ < 1 be the rank-deficit parameter, η ≥ 0 a frame-error parameter and 0 ≤ e ≤ 1/4 the second error parameter. With these hypotheses, SlopeIneq asks for

s − log |W| − [4bF log(1 + H/bF) + (η + 4√e)H]/(1 − δ) ≤ μ(R∨).

If bF = 0 the first product inside the brackets is zero, also its limit from positive bF. This inequality places the same dual-lattice slope appearing in the divisibility inequality on the opposite side. Combining its lower bound with divisibility's upper bound, the rank mean comparison, and the counting inequalities bounds the finite-place gain by M plus errors. It also supplies bounds for the error parameters, so large values of H can be multiplied by small η and √e. Exact frame conditions and ceiling[362] Combining the lower and upper bounds[363]

5.5Eliminating the two auxiliary lattice quantities

Write G for the weighted finite-place gain called Ga, F for the separate finite-place correction Fo, Eu for the word’s exponent sum, and μR for μ(R∨). At a fixed translation and word, write Qu for its source-lattice mean muM, Lu for its explicit loss Lo5, and Derr for the divisibility error. The two inequalities entering the proof are

μ(Nu) ≥ Qu + G + F − Eu − Lu,   μR + hu − F ≤ SD − A log Tu + Derr.

Solve the second inequality for F and insert its lower bound in the first. The word height then cancels upon passing to μ(Nu) − hu. Average with the word ranks. Using log Tu ≥ λ, the exponent upper bound and the lower bound on Qu gives s ≥ G + μR − M − errors. Now rearrange the slope inequality above as s ≤ μR + log |W| + frame error. Comparing eliminates μR, leaving G ≤ M + errors. This explains both the sign of the finite-place correction and the need to bound the same dual lattice from both sides. The word-independent error called K0v5 is exactly the sum of AEc, Derr, the exponent error mCEB₀, and the source-slope error Cslope|Top|aLa(1+m/k). The rank-averaged word losses and the frame error still appear separately. 5.6Why the slope bound contains a logarithm

Think of a lattice through its finite list of Harder–Narasimhan slopes, each repeated according to rank. A step in its filtration contains the directions whose slopes meet a given threshold. For a slope λ of the underlying real lattice the arithmetic normalization is 2λ + cK, with the same field constant for all words and the target. The resulting list has arithmetic mean equal to the lattice's mean slope. For the source lattices subtract each height allowance and concatenate the lists over all words. Their mean is s and every entry is at most s + bF. If a fraction p lies below s − τ, for τ ≥ 0, then the mean is at most p(s − τ) + (1 − p)(s + bF). Rearranging gives p ≤ bF/(bF + τ) when the denominator is positive. If both quantities vanish, all slopes equal s and the strict lower tail is empty. This bounds the rank lost when we discard low-slope steps in the source. The filtered source ranks[366] Bounds for the mean and maximum[367]

What happens to the remaining directions under the word maps? At threshold s − τ, take the sum of the images of the retained steps in R∨. A slope inequality for the maps, together with their height bounds, places this sum in the target filtration step. The source estimates its codimension using a matrix calculation at one infinite place. With p bounded as above, the resulting fraction of target slopes below the threshold is at most

ω(τ) = [η + 4bF/(bF + τ) + 4√e]/(1 − δ).

The matrix calculation uses bounds on traces and on Hilbert–Schmidt deviations after restriction to the selected columns. These estimates connect the dimensions of the source steps to the dimension of their combined image. Counting the target slopes below threshold now amounts to counting the dimensions missing from its filtration step. Inclusion of the image[368] The target count[369] Matrix estimates used in the ramified case[370]

Let ν run through the normalized target slopes with multiplicity. The lower-slope bound says ν ≥ s − H. Consequently the interval of τ in [0, H] for which ν < s − τ has length max(s − ν, 0). Average these lengths over the finite list. Their integral representation, followed by the bound above, gives

s − mean(ν) ≤ mean[max(s − ν, 0)] = ∫0H fraction{ν < s − τ} dτ ≤ ∫0H ω(τ) dτ.

For example, set s = 4 and take the three numbers 1, 3, 5 with H = 3. Two lie below 4 − τ for 0 ≤ τ < 1, and one lies below it for 1 ≤ τ < 3. The integral of the fraction is (2/3)·1 + (1/3)·2 = 4/3. This equals the average of the positive deficits 3, 1, 0. The signed mean deficit is only 1, since the last value exceeds 4. This finite list illustrates the integration step.

For bF > 0, integrating bF/(bF + τ) gives bF log(1 + H/bF). For bF = 0 this contribution vanishes. The two constant terms in ω integrate to (η + 4√e)H/(1 − δ). Since mean(ν) = μ(R∨), the calculation actually proves the bound without subtracting log |W|. The later theorem uses the displayed weaker version by subtracting the nonnegative logarithm of the number of words. 5.8How many columns survive the ramification conditions?

For a word u, write T for its prime level, f for the number of selected places over T, dfull for the dimension at level zero and dram for the dimension left after imposing the local conditions. 5.9Why each orbit is a product of residue groups

At each selected place the residue field has T elements. Its unit group H has T − 1 elements. The level-zero forms admit a model as complex functions on a finite set X. An element of H in one coordinate acts by a local dilation, also called a diamond operator. The operator Nv sums all these dilations in the coordinate v. Under the model, its kernel consists of functions whose sum along that coordinate is zero at every point. The ramified subspace is the intersection of these kernels. The function model and the action[389] Translation of the norm operator[390] The intersection of kernels[391]

Freeness uses arithmetic. Suppose a tuple of local multipliers fixes a level class. Represent it by an adelic element δ, whose components at the two auxiliary type primes are the identity. The power δT−1 belongs to the level subgroup, since the residues of all its multipliers have that power equal to 1. The diamond operator normalizes the level, so the same power of δκ belongs to the level for every level element κ. Fixing the class supplies a rational element γ from the double-coset relation. The admissible stabilizer gives γT−1 = 1. At each of the two distinct auxiliary primes p, the local reduction calculation kills every power of γ of order coprime to p. To see the force of having two primes, write T − 1 = pam with p ∤ m. The first condition kills γpa, whose order divides m. Now γ has order dividing pa, which is coprime to the second prime. Hence γ = 1 and δ itself lies in the level subgroup. Each local multiplier fixes a nonzero level functional killed by T. A multiplier c must therefore satisfy c ≡ 1 mod T. The tuple is the identity. From a fixed class to rational torsion[392] Reduction at the two primes[393] The two-prime argument[394] Reading the multiplier on the functional[395] Application to the tuple[396]

Choosing orbit representatives now identifies X with Q × Hf, where Q indexes the orbits of the function model. Its size includes the multiplicity of the value space. On each orbit a function has (T − 1)f entries before imposing any sums. The class orbits and value-space multiplicity[397] The model for split level data[398] Bijection from freeness[399]

5.10Counting the independent values

Keep only the entries indexed by tuples with every coordinate different from the identity. They determine a function with vanishing line sums uniquely. To recover an entry with an identity coordinate, it must be the negative of the sum of the other entries on that line. Each of those entries has one fewer identity coordinate, so induction recovers the full table. Conversely, to extend a unit value at such a tuple a, use the product over coordinates v of (1hv=av − 1hv=1). It sums to zero along every coordinate and restricts to the unit value at a and zero at every other retained tuple. Taking linear combinations extends arbitrary data. Thus there are (T − 2)f independent values on each orbit. Products with zero coordinate sums[400] Uniqueness by induction[401] Extension and the dimension formula[402]

dfull = |Q| (T − 1)f,   dram = |Q| (T − 2)f.

A four-by-four check. Take one orbit, T = 5 and f = 2. Order the four residues in both coordinates as 2, 3, 4, 1. Put ones on the diagonal of the first three-by-three block, zeros in its other six entries. Zero row sums force the first three entries of the last column to be −1. Zero column sums force the first three entries of the last row to be −1. Both conditions put 3 in the final corner. The nine free entries determine all sixteen. The eight row and column equations have one redundancy because summing all rows also sums all columns. The lost fraction is 7/16. Restriction to the free entries[403] Dimension as a proportion[404]

For a nonzero full space and T ≥ 3, Bernoulli’s inequality gives

1 − dram/dfull = 1 − (1 − 1/(T − 1))f ≤ f/(T − 1) ≤ 2f/T.

The scale conditions give T ≥ bm/2 ≥ b, with b = exp(xε), b ≥ 3 and m ≥ 2. Thus dfull − dram ≤ de dfull for de = 2f/b. The undivided inequality also holds if the full space is zero. For each fixed family with ε > 0, one threshold works for every later x and every family index. The number f can depend on that index, but the same de works for all its words. Eventually f ≤ k ≤ x5, 2f ≤ exp(xε/2), and xε ≥ 4xε/8. Consequently √de ≤ exp(−xε/4) ≤ exp(−xε/8). Put Ex = exp(−xε/8). To obtain a bound common to all indices at this x, the proof enlarges the rank-loss cap to Ex² and the separate matrix-error cap to 2Ex². The rank term in the frame error 5σ + 3Ex now has the same value at every index. The common frame calculation supplies the diagonal and off-diagonal bounds on the full period matrices. 5.12What controls the variation of the prime level?

The word-to-word part of Count5 uses a Vandermonde product V(z) = ∏a<b(za − zb) in the decreasing real parameters at a place. Its logarithm is a sum over pairs. For the first row a = 0 the two compared gaps are each at least 4kΔ and change by at most Δ. The variation of each logarithm is at most 1/(4k). For a ≥ 1 the gaps are at least 3(b − a)Δ and change by at most 2Δ, giving 2/[3(b − a)] per pair. Both bounds follow by integrating 1/t between the gaps. A harmonic sum over b bounds the logarithmic variation at a place by 1/4 + (2/3)k(1 + log k). Summing over f places and applying the factor 1/(fk) in the level parameter leaves variation of order log k. The shared auxiliary factor cancels when the two word windows are compared. The absolute bounds for each word also use a torus-pair estimate involving the mass, volume and formal degree. 5.13How close are the period operators to a common orthonormal frame?

Two periods can each preserve lengths and still take their values on the same line. A slope estimate that uses many words therefore needs two measurements. For a fixed family member let Pu carry the full complex space of word u, of dimension du, into one Hilbert space. Normalize by the real number cu, the product of its two unfolding volumes divided by the product of its column representation dimensions over the infinite places. The operator from the space of v to the space of u is

Kuv = (cucv)−1/2 Pu∗Pv,   Q(A) = ∑j ‖Aej‖².

Here the ej run through an orthonormal basis of the domain. For u = v we measure Q(Kuu − I). For distinct words we measure Q(Kuv), which adds the squared absolute values of all correlations between the two normalized families of columns. The estimates are for the full word dimension. 5.14Separating the nonidentity terms with zero Gram label

The geometric expansion of Kuv converges absolutely. Write Buv for its subseries of terms with Gram label zero and with the identity excluded. Set D∗ equal to the positive reference size for the target dimension and ξ = exp(−kf log k). The proof uses four estimates. On different words the subseries vanishes, and the remaining squared norm is at most (1 + b−6)dudv/D∗. On the diagonal it gives

Q(Buu) ≤ ξdu,   Q(Kuu − Buu − I) ≤ Γdu²/D∗.

The four estimates have different suppliers. Local types kill the unwanted off-diagonal terms. A positive-kernel estimate controls their diagonal subseries. The selected different-word estimate controls the rest off the diagonal. On the diagonal a geometric row estimate controls what is left after subtracting the identity. Absolute convergence permits these subtractions. The selected subseries[418] The four inequalities[419] Where each supplier enters[420] Normalizations of the errors[421]

Why can a pair of words have a zero orbital term?

Fix two distinct words u and v in the selected family. Their local unitary representations have different weight parameters at every infinite place. Examine a single nonidentity term with Gram label zero in Buv. It compares a flag with a translate of the other flag. Call the pair relevant when the differentials of their two characters agree on every common infinitesimal unipotent direction. There are two ways for its orbital integral P to vanish. Where the word separation enters[422] The relevance condition[423]

If relevance fails, one direction gives unequal phases. In fact the proof rescales that direction so that, with N infinite places, the difference in the two character exponents is πi/N at each place. The product of the first character with the conjugate of the second therefore takes the value exp(πi) = −1. This character is trivial on the rational lattice. Averaging over its compact quotient in the common unipotent group gives zero, since translating the character average by that element changes its sign. The orbital integrand transforms by exactly this character, so the orbital integral vanishes. Choosing the direction and its scale[424] The phase difference[425] The character in the integral[426]

For a relevant pair with Gram label zero, the geometric normal form gives a positive orthonormal frame perpendicular to both flag subspaces at each infinite place. Write its columns as W and the ambient Hermitian form as J, so W∗JW = I. Every M ∈ U(k) extends to a symmetry fixing those subspaces pointwise. Indeed, put

H = I + W(M − I)W∗J.   HW = WM,   Hy = y whenever W∗Jy = 0.

On the frame this map preserves the inner product because M is unitary, and on its orthogonal complement it is the identity. The other flag sees the action as CMC∗ for a fixed unitary matrix C at that place. Invariance of the orbital integral under the pointwise stabilizer gives covariance between these two actions. This uses the existence of the fundamental domain and integrability of the orbital kernel. The two corrected frames[427] The extension formula[428] The unitary comparison[429] The two actions[430] Covariance of the integral[431]

Choose one infinite place and let M vary only there. Fix arbitrary vectors in every other tensor factor on each side. Let Su and Sv insert a local vector into those fixed tensors. For A = Su∗PSv, covariance reads

πu(M)A = Aπv(CMC∗),   πu(M)R = Rπv(M),   R = Aπv(C).

A nonzero R would be an isomorphism. Its kernel and image are invariant, and the two finite-dimensional representations are irreducible. An isomorphism preserves the weights of the diagonal torus, including the distinguished extremal weight that determines each type. The unequal parameters rule this out. Hence R = 0 and A = 0. Varying the fixed tensors shows that every matrix coefficient of P between pure tensors vanishes. They span both spaces. Can a scalar unitary distinguish these two types of U(2)?

On the determinant line and on Sym²(ℂ²), the scalar zI acts by z². Suppose an intertwiner sends a generator of the determinant line to a quadratic tensor w. Every diag(z,z−1) with |z| = 1 fixes w. In the basis e₁², e₁e₂, e₂², the three eigenvalues are z², 1 and z−2. Thus w is a multiple of e₁e₂. Swapping the basis vectors fixes that monomial and multiplies the determinant by −1. Equivariance gives w = −w, so w = 0.

Both cases kill each selected term individually, so their sum Buv is zero. The other terms still contribute to Kuv. The separate different-word estimate bounds the squared norm of Kuv − Buv, and substituting zero gives the bound for the full block. Fix distinct words u and v and put Δ = dudv/D∗. The preceding argument removes the nonidentity terms whose geometric Gram label is zero. The remaining sum, called K₀, contains the identity part and two groups of terms with nonzero label. The identity part also vanishes for this calculation. Call the two groups G (generic) and N (nongeneric). Genericity tests a pair of lattice flags. Their integral span has a saturation, obtained by intersecting its field span with the ambient lattice. At primes away from the level, genericity requires that the original span already give the saturation locally. At primes dividing the level, one admissible matrix must supply the saturation using the corrected frame differences divided by the level. A term is generic when a representative passes these tests. Each term t contributes a vector vt supported on one pair of lattices. Its row records those lattices and a finite index i. For either group S, form ai by summing its vectors with index i. In the square of that sum, terms with the same index but different lattice pairs have disjoint support. Absolute convergence permits regrouping, so only ordered pairs in the same row contribute. With Γ₁ the positive Gram normalization, the resulting energy is

Φ(S) = Γ₁ ∑i ‖ai‖² = Γ₁ ∑s,t ∈ S, same row Re ⟨vs, vt⟩.

Individual inner products can have either sign. To bound the sum, the proof groups pairs by their corank s₀ = k − dim Θ, where Θ consists of first components of vector pairs compatible with the two flags and their comparison map. On a common row with both Gram labels nonzero, s₀ ≥ 1. Among generic pairs of corank one, the scalar pairs preserve the two coefficients of the distinguished flag vectors under comparison. The large-corank estimate bounds the sum of absolute inner products over all same-row pairs of nonzero-label terms of corank at least two by εΔ, including the factor Γ₁. Thus each group can use this bound on its own subset. In G, the nonscalar corank-one pairs cost at most another εΔ in absolute value. The signed sum of the scalar pairs is at most AΔ. In N, one signed bound ε′Δ covers all corank-one pairs. These are the only cases, giving

Φ(G) ≤ (A + 2ε)Δ,   Φ(N) ≤ (ε + ε′)Δ.

The common Gram matrix converts each energy to an upper bound on the squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of its operator sum, with a factor P. The triangle inequality then gives the retained block bound

‖K₀‖² ≤ (√[P(A + 2ε)] + √[P(ε + ε′)])² Δ ≤ (1 + b−6)Δ.

Why take the square roots? Consider two contributions along one unit vector, with coefficients 1 and 1/10. Their squared norms are 1 and 1/100, but their sum has squared norm 121/100. 6Theta lifts, local factors and the Galois input

How can a theorem attaching Galois representations in odd dimension give one in even dimension? Lift the same automorphic representation twice to a larger odd rank, adding different character lists each time. The shared part can then be recovered. Both global theta integrals must produce a nonzero form for this argument to start.

What is being lifted? · Two parallel lifts · Recovering the even-dimensional row · The iterated chain · Split and inert places · The finite test vector · Real places · Continuation · Split lattice calculation · Inert cell calculation

6.1What is being lifted?

A Hermitian form measures lengths using both a field and its conjugation. On two complex coordinates the example is ⟨x,y⟩ = x₁y₁ + x₂y₂. Its unitary group consists of the changes of coordinates preserving this pairing. For a number field we can make such a change at each place. An adelic group element collects these choices, integral at almost every finite place. A rational change of coordinates gives the same change simultaneously in all completions.

An automorphic form here is a function on the adelic group, invariant under those rational changes on the left and satisfying additional finiteness and regularity conditions. Translating its argument on the right produces a space of functions carrying a group action. The irreducible space being lifted is U, and φ is one vector in it. A theta kernel converts φ into a function on another group by integration. To show that this conversion retains some information, one proves that a resulting vector has positive squared norm. At a good finite prime the commuting Hecke operators then provide a list of spectral parameters, with multiplicities, which can be compared on the two sides.

6.2Two parallel lifts to odd rank

Let E be a CM field, a totally imaginary quadratic extension of its totally real subfield F. The version used here assumes that E/F is unramified at all finite places, that E contains a square root of a negative rational integer, and that [F : ℚ] is even. At every nonsplit finite place the underlying prime of F has odd residue characteristic, norm greater than three and does not divide the absolute different of F. Take an even rank n ≥ 1 and an automorphic representation U of the definite unitary group of rank n. Fix its highest weights λ at the complex embeddings and a finite split place w₀ of E. Both targets are definite skew-Hermitian models of rank D = n + t, an odd integer above the threshold. Each lift uses its own compatible pair of splitting Hecke characters. The proof takes a common lower bound b for the components of λ at the chosen complex embedding above each real place and chooses their target exponents so that mW,j(v) ≤ 2b − D. Thus every required archimedean inequality D + mW,j(v) ≤ 2λv,k holds. Applying the same rank theorem once for each pair produces U₁ and U₂. 7The arithmetic balance

At d the inertia subgroup has order two, so averaging replaces 2 by 1 at each matching element outside Φ. Each such weight contributes log d times its value. For v = wρ the identity (a/n − v)+ = v(a/(v n) − 1)+ changes the scale to y = a/v. Terms beyond the cutoff vanish. Write Gψ(y) for the centered ramp. For a nontrivial ψ it sums the von Mangoldt weight, multiplied by the local character value and y/n − 1, over 1 ≤ n ≤ y, then adds y ℓ(ψ). For the trivial character it uses the centered zeta ramp. Substitution gives the following main term, where γ is Euler’s constant. The centered character ramp[753] Main term and remainder[754]

M = a log a − (1 + γ)a − (a/|Φ|) ∑ρ ∈ Φ log wρ + a ℓ(χC).

The trivial character gives the first three terms. For the other characters the centering contributes −a ℓ(ψ). Summing the conjugate phases over the complementary half of E kills the nonconstant characters except χC, whose sum is −|Φ|. This accounts for the plus sign. The pairing of the two halves permutes the weight indices, giving precisely the average of their logarithms. The remainder A − M is the same character average with centered ramps in the summands. This proves the analytic identity at fixed host data. Identifying the degrees, periods, heights and covolumes of the geometric construction with this particular M is an additional theorem. Balance identity and sign calculation[755] The identification consumed by the geometric estimate[756]

At one translation the lattice calculation uses the sum over all sampled indices t and stages j. Its total amplitude was denoted by A = ∑t at. Here the object being summed is the count At,j just computed, and its main term is Mt,j. The two identifications together make the geometric residual exactly ∑t,j (At,j − Re Mt,j). This equality is what allows the character average to use the geometric bound. Identification of the aggregate main term[757] The residual before averaging[758]

7.2Which characters survive?

Let A0 be a subgroup of H. For ψ a character of E, put Sψ = ∑u ∈ A₀ ψ(0, −u). Translation by any v ∈ A0 permutes this sum and multiplies it by ψ(0, −v). Thus the sum vanishes whenever one of these multipliers differs from one. Otherwise it equals |A0|. For e1(τ) = ((1,0),τ) and s ∈ A0, the corresponding shifted sum acquires the phase ψ(e1(τ)). Summing over s ∈ T2 ⊆ A0 and averaging over subgroup translations therefore contributes a density δ2/2 with δ2 = |T2|/|H|. The two in the denominator comes from |Φ| = 2|H|. Translation and density identities[759]

For example, take H = ℤ/4ℤ and A0 = {0, 2}. On H the four characters are ψj(h) = exp(2πijh/4) for j = 0, 1, 2, 3. Averaging ψj over A0 gives (1 + (−1)j)/2. The odd indices cancel and the even ones survive with value 1. If T2 contains one element, its contribution occupies one of the eight positions in Φ. The factor 1/8 comes from that count, independently of which surviving character is evaluated.

At a scale x ≥ 3, fix a loss ε > 0, a real sampling weight c with |c| ≤ 1, and a finite sample T ⊆ H. The survivors form the annihilator Ψ of A0. A further selection K ⊆ Ψ retains characters used in the target. For these the source imposes ψ(sgc0) = 1 and includes the trivial character. Among retained characters, a character trivial on all of H receives weight 1. The others receive c. Call these weights ωψ. For retained characters nontrivial on H, the sum over T of ψ(0,τ) differs from c|T| in norm by at most M0x−1+ε|T|, where M0 also bounds |Ψ|. The constants bounding ℓ on retained nontrivial and discarded characters are respectively K0 and CE log x. The sum of norms of the discarded centered ramps is denoted Σ. Orthogonality by itself leaves this last error to be paid. Weights, discarded sum and sampling assumptions[760]

7.3Dividing the error by the observed weight

Write n = |H|, t = |T|, v = |T2|, m for the length of the chain and b for its positive weight scale. At a translation τ the measurement uses an amplitude aτ with |aτ/b − x| ≤ 1. In the realized chain aE is the size parameter Dd.a, and the adjustable positive parameter k is real. For each subgroup translation, Err bounds the sum, over all t samples and m chain positions, of A − Re M. Weights and translated gaps[761]

For each subgroup translation u, the local comparison keeps the indices ((0,1),s + u) with s ∈ T2. The source calls these the thick indices. At those indices b ≤ w ≤ b + η + 1 with η ≥ 0. Replacing w by b changes the weighted ramp by at most 3(x + 1)(η + 1). At each other index in Φ, w ≤ 2b′. The parameters satisfy b′, X′ > 0 and b′X′ ≤ xb, so aτ/w ≥ X′/3. On this range assume ‖Gψ(y)‖ ≤ yθ with θ ≥ 0. Omitting that term costs at most (x + 1)bθ. With f = |Φ|, the normalized character sum multiplies the sum of these two allowances by at most 2f. The conditions 6f(x + 1)(η + 1) ≤ b/x and 2f(x + 1)θ ≤ 1/x give a total allowance of 2b/x per measurement. Termwise comparison[762] The two local cost conditions[763] Thick indices[764]

At the central scale define the signed real signal B = ∑ψ ∈ K ωψ Re Gψ(x) − Σ, where Σ = ∑ψ ∈ Ψ ∖ K ‖Gψ(x)‖. Also put Q = t m b. The estimate takes the form

Q (v/2n)(B − 4X) ≤ Err + 2Q/x,   X = x1/2+ε.

For positive observed weight Qv/(2n), direct division shows what an error costs. The upper bound for B is 4X + (2n/v)(Err/Q + 2/x). In the four-translation example v/(2n) = 1/8, so a unit of normalized error Err/Q increases the allowance by eight. A large negative B already satisfies the inequality. Its use later in the proof therefore requires the specific linear combinations of characters that recover the desired upper bound.

For each surviving character, the source bounds the real part of its phase-weighted sample sum from below, comparing each aτ/b with x. After summation the lower bound is t(B − 4X). Averaging the local upper bounds over the subgroup introduces the factor v/(2n). The signed lower and upper estimates then give the displayed inequality. The norms in Σ permit the discarded characters to contribute with either sign. Single-character lower bound[765] From translated gaps to a scalar inequality[766] Application of the scalar lemma[767]

Assume x ≥ 3, ε > 0, C ≥ 0, b > 0, n ≥ 1, 0 ≤ aE ≤ 2x b. The scalar size hypothesis bounds Err by xCε times the sum of four quantities. The right column gives each quotient after division by Q. Complete scalar hypotheses[768]

ContributionAfter division by t m b
t aEaE/(m b)
t aEm²/kaEm/(b k)
m(2n m b xε)2(n/t)m xε
m v k b xε/(n²x−ε)(v/t)(k/n²)x2ε

The leading scales are consequently x/m, xm/k, m, k/n². Balancing the first and third suggests m near √x. This heuristic by itself supplies neither admissible ranks nor densities. The size lemma actually assumes

x1/2−ε ≤ m ≤ x1/2+ε/2,   xm ≤ k ≤ n²x1/2−ε,
t ≥ ½n x−ε/8,   x−ε ≤ v/n ≤ 1,   x3ε/8 ≥ 26.

These conditions give Q > 0. Set Y = x1/2+13ε/8. The first quotient is at most 2X ≤ 2Y. The second is at most 2 by the lower bound on k. For the third use n/t ≤ 2xε/8 and the upper bound on m to get 4Y. For the fourth, v ≤ n gives v/t ≤ 2xε/8. Its upper bound is 2x1/2+9ε/8 ≤ 2Y. Altogether Err/Q ≤ 10xCεY. This is where the admissible interval for k matters. Both endpoints must hold at the same scale. Four separate bounds[769]

Since 2/x ≤ 1 and xCεY ≥ 1, the scalar inequality gives (v/n)(B − 4X) ≤ 22xCεY. Divide by the positive density, whose reciprocal is at most xε. Then B ≤ 26x1/2+(C+21/8)ε. The last threshold absorbs 26 and gives the exponent 1/2 + (C + 3)ε. The written proof of ch_core passes the signed B and the averaged inequality directly to proposition_size_bound. Its proof calls the four component bounds in the same file. The scalar size lemma[770]

7.4What does one arithmetic measurement buy?

Fix a level, a scale x in its arithmetic window and the sampling data at that scale. At translation σ, subtract the predicted main term from the prime-power count and sum over the samples and chain stages. Call this real difference Δσ. The lattice argument gives an upper bound Err for each Δσ. The character calculation reads the same differences in the opposite direction. Write B for the weighted sum of the retained real parts after subtracting the allowance for discarded characters.

Set X = x½+ε and write Q for the total weight. It is the product of the number of samples, the number of stages and the weight per measurement. The average runs over the translation subgroup. At each translation the calculation keeps v of the 2n weight positions, a fraction v/(2n). Replacing their individual weights by a common weight and bounding the omitted terms costs the additive 2Q/x. Upper bound for one translation · The averaged comparison

Q · [v/(2n)](B − 4X) ≤ meanσ Δσ + 2Q/x ≤ Err + 2Q/x.
Which part of this chain can a normalized theta coefficient justify?

In a differentiated theta series, the coefficient of a monomial of degree j in one variable is multiplied by j! when its jth derivative is evaluated at zero. After the section and its coordinates have been normalized, a valuation estimate on that derivative controls divisibility of a lattice-map entry. This contributes to the upper bound on Δσ. The other use of theta, constructing nonzero global lifts, supplies the Galois row used to select a window. There the weighted cohomology lengths fit within √b, with b the weight per measurement. Setting Err equal to √b would drop the other costs of the lattice comparison. The factorial in the entry · How the lifts supply the row · Where the length bound enters

If the total allowance is 60, how far above 4X can B lie?

For an arithmetic check on the division, take Q = 80, v/(2n) = ¼ and Err + 2Q/x = 60. The observed weight is 20, giving B ≤ 4X + 3. A value 100 below 4X also satisfies the inequality. Recovering the fixed family sum requires adding back the allowance for discarded characters. The analytic test then uses the positive part of that family sum. Recovery of the level sum · The positive part in the pole test

Would measurements at both ends of the interval suffice?

A continuous positive bump between the endpoints can have any prescribed integral while vanishing at both ends. The arithmetic construction provides estimates throughout one interval for the same level sum. Passing to u = log x gives the integral bound on that interval, and arbitrarily distant such intervals are available. Carry the bound across the whole interval.

7.5Recovering the level sum

For a level Λ of order o, core_gm applies the preceding argument with c = 1/(3o + 1) and M0 = 4o. The hypotheses EAtH and CoreAtH supply the local character estimates and compatible chain data at the chosen scale. In particular eD + eL ≥ 0 and the error exponent C can be taken as eD + eL + 3. Each discarded character contributes at most x1/2+ε in norm. Counting the entire annihilator bounds Σ by 4o x1/2+ε. Thus GΛ is at most (1 + 4o)x1/2+(eD+eL+6)ε. Choosing x large enough that xε ≥ 1 + 4o gives

GΛ(x) ≤ x1/2+(eD+eL+7)ε.

The exponent applies to scales carrying the required data. A fixed ε allows thresholds depending on the level and constants, uniformly in the later choices of host and sample. The window construction supplies such scales. The level bound[771] Discarded characters[772] Transport to family windows[773]

The third-place construction used by the final theorem chooses eD = 2 and eL = 0. The argument order is visible in topDesWin, which passes those two real numbers on as the family exponents. This specialization gives 1/2 + 9ε. Parameter choice[586] Transport of the exponents[774]
