8Supplying the arithmetic hypotheses

The arithmetic estimate uses many fields and many primes. To control their total contribution, the proof bounds the lengths of cohomology groups on carefully chosen intervals. This is where one must keep track of which parameters have already been fixed when a field or window is chosen.

What length measures · The allowance per measurement · The three contributions · Tower generators · Descent · Selecting the interval · The degree-two bound · Detecting cycles · Counting faces · The plus bound · Trace congruences · The minus bound · The Frobenius test · Choosing both primes · The final window

8.1From Galois representations to window data

Over a CM field E, the row hypothesis applies to a regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representation of positive rank a. A CM field is a totally imaginary quadratic extension of a totally real field. In this setting a polarization relates a representation to a twist of its conjugate dual. For each allowed ℓ-adic coefficient realization, the conclusion gives a representation of the absolute Galois group on an a-dimensional ℓ-adic vector space, a weight and Hodge–Tate weight data. Its package of requirements includes continuity, semisimplicity and prescribed local compatibility. The local theory uses both places above ℓ and places away from ℓ. The window construction uses this row directly and to obtain its open-image input, together with the base-change theorem. Galois row hypotheses and conclusion[775] Construction from the row[776]

The separate chapter on the two theta lifts explains the Galois input. For the derivative estimate used on the geometric side, see the factorial gain and the mixed-coordinate correction. The estimate on cohomology below has different indices and quantifiers.

8.2What the good arithmetic window controls

One can first think of a degree-one cohomology class as a way of assigning a value to each symmetry. A cocycle satisfies c(gh) = c(g) + g·c(h). Two choices give the same class if they differ by g ↦ g·a − a. For the group of order two acting trivially on ℤ/4, the choice at its generator must double to zero. The two possibilities 0 and 2 give exactly two classes. In the arithmetic problem the group is a Galois group, the action includes a twist and one retains classes whose restrictions vanish at the specified places. This is the reason a kernel of a restriction map occurs below.

We measure a finite ℤℓ-module by its length. Filter it until each successive quotient has order ℓ. If there are d quotients, its order is ℓd. Both ℤ/ℓ² and (ℤ/ℓ)² have length two, although they require different numbers of generators. Later the tower estimate uses both quantities. Over a coefficient ring with residue field of size ℓf, each quotient instead contributes f to the base-ℓ logarithm of the order.

Fix a number field E and a rational prime ℓ. The coefficient module here is the discrete quotient ℚℓ/ℤℓ. A Tate twist changes the scalar by which Galois acts. If the ℓ-adic cyclotomic character is χcyc, the action on this quotient uses χcyc−j for the integer j in the window sum. With this action the cocycle rule above becomes c(gh) = c(g) + χcyc(g)−jc(h). Vanishing on restriction means the restricted cocycle becomes a coboundary.

The source uses the Galois group with ramification allowed in the specified set of primes above ℓ. The set S in LData is precisely the finite places dividing ℓ. One chooses a place of the algebraic closure above each member and restricts to the corresponding decomposition group. Write hℓ,j for the ℤℓ-module length of the subgroup Sha of these locally trivial degree-one classes. The related degree-two group has coefficients ℤℓ(j + 1). Thus the locally trivial subgroup within degree one is the intersection of the kernels of those local restriction maps. The length bounded by VVle is its ℤℓ-module length. Intersection of restriction kernels[777] Local data, twists and lengths[778] Maps to the global Galois group[779]

Given t and B, VVle demands finiteness of every hℓ,j for 1 ≤ j < t, for all allowed choices of closure and local data. For every finite set P of rational primes it also requires

∑ℓ ∈ P (log ℓ) ∑1 ≤ j < t hℓ,j ≤ B.

The field varies with a primitive character ψ, the height in a cyclotomic tower, and two auxiliary primes q,d. In a cyclotomic field containing the relevant roots of unity, IsChiField specifies the subgroup fixing E by the intersection of four conditions on the exponent of an automorphism: congruence to ±1 modulo 2e+2, ψ(a) = 1, and two quadratic-symbol conditions at q and d. For a fixed ψ and 0 < ε < 1/52, choose any integer function e(x) satisfying x2+8ε ≤ 2e(x) ≤ 2x2+8ε for all x ≥ 1. Then VWin supplies J ≥ 1 and a threshold X0. For every X beyond it and every admissible pair (q,d) at scale X1/J, there is Y ≥ X1/J with Y² ≤ X. Throughout [Y,Y²], every such field satisfies the length bound for t = ⌊x401⌋ and B = exp(xε/2). An admissible pair must obey the prime, congruence, divisibility and logarithmic size conditions of WinPair. Field, auxiliary primes and complete quantifiers[780]

8.3Splitting the obstruction by the action of conjugation

There is a different estimate for each of three parts of the cohomological sum. To see where they come from, fix a CM field in the construction, a twist index j and an odd prime ℓ. Complex conjugation on the CM field induces a linear involution c on the degree-one cohomology. Its action preserves the locally trivial subgroup. Put s = (−1)j. Because 2 is a unit in ℤℓ, every locally trivial class v has a decomposition

v = ½(v + scv) + ½(v − scv).

Applying c to the first summand multiplies it by s, and applying it to the second multiplies it by −s. Both still lie in the subgroup. A vector in both eigenspaces satisfies 2sv = 0, hence vanishes. The sum is direct, so the full module length equals the sum of its two eigenspace lengths. The name “plus” in the source means eigenvalue (−1)j; for odd j this is the −1 eigenspace. At ℓ = 2 the projectors involve a forbidden division, and the full module is estimated separately. Direct-sum construction[781] Conjugation and the two parities[782]

On the joint window there are bounds B2 on the sum of full lengths at ℓ = 2, and B+ and B− on the logarithmically weighted odd-prime sums of the two corresponding lengths. Each comes with finiteness for its twists and primes. Length additivity gives finiteness of the full group at odd primes as well. For any finite prime set, split off 2 if present, and add the two odd-prime inequalities term by term. This proves the bound B2 log 2 + B+ + B−. It explains why the factor log 2 appears only on the first term. Finiteness hypotheses and combination theorem[783]

8.4Putting the three estimates on one interval

Existence of two arbitrarily distant intervals separately would give no control of their intersection. The source instead constructs a window satisfying a specified condition IsBWindow, which includes a bound at 2 and bounds on certain layers of auxiliary prime towers. The plus estimate is proved on every window satisfying this condition, once the same prime pair is large enough. Choose the maximum of the two thresholds for X, and an upper bound for the finitely many forbidden-size parameters for the two primes. An interval supplied by the first theorem then satisfies the second theorem with the same endpoints, field and tower level. The minus estimate applies to the composite CM field without any further window choice. Definition of the common window[784] Quantifiers of the plus estimate[785] Joint window assembly[786]

Write NE for the conductor of the field, t for the twist cutoff and u = NEt. On the accepted window u ≥ 1 and log u ≤ 2xε/4. Indeed NE ≤ 2e+2Nψqd. Taking logarithms, the page bound and t ≤ x401 contribute at most a fixed constant plus a constant times log x; the pair satisfies log(qd) ≤ xε/4. The first terms are eventually absorbed in a second xε/4. With constants C,K fixed before x, the three bounds take the form

B2 = exp(x4ε/5),   B− ≤ K exp(8xε/4),
B+ = uC + C exp(x4ε/5).

For u ≥ 1, uC ≤ exp(2|C|xε/4). Every exponent on the right of the displayed estimates is o(xε) for fixed ε > 0. Beyond a common threshold each exponential is at most exp(xε/4), and the sum of the fixed nonnegative prefactors, including log 2 and absolute values for constants, is itself at most exp(xε/4). Their product proves the required exp(xε/2). This comparison is uniform over fields obeying the conductor bound. Conductor estimate[787] Minus contribution[788] Uniform error ceiling[789] Assembly for the chosen field[790]

The tower estimate uses a bound on degree-two cohomology, Poitou–Tate duality, local finiteness, local Tate duality and the Ferrero–Washington theorem. The plus contribution also uses separate representation counts. The following argument explains how the number of generators of a tower module controls the choice of the common interval. Inputs to the tower estimate[791] Use at twist cutoff exponent 401[792]

8.5What Ferrero–Washington supplies in this proof

A generator bound limits how many independent ℓ-adic directions can contribute to the growth of a cohomology group. The argument starts with the ideal class groups of the number fields in the finite layers of a cyclotomic tower, passes to a single module for the infinite tower, and then recovers the length at any chosen finite layer as a quotient of that module. The class group of a number field is the group of its nonzero fractional ideals modulo principal ideals.

Write Cl(L) for the ideal class group of a number field L, written additively. The number of independent characters of order ℓ depends on Cl(L)/ℓCl(L). For an abelian extension K/ℚ containing a primitive ℓth root of unity, or a primitive fourth root of unity at ℓ = 2, the statement called Published.FerreroWashington gives a single integer r such that

|Cl(K(μℓⁿ))/ℓCl(K(μℓⁿ))| ≤ ℓr   for every n ≥ 0.

Here μℓⁿ denotes the roots of unity of order dividing ℓn. The constant can depend on ℓ and K. The name Published occurs in the type of the result. The actual window proof passes the theorem FW.ferreroWashington, whose written body constructs r. Class-group statement[793] Construction of the exponent[794] Use by the window proof[792]

First work in the full cyclotomic fields L = ℚ(μfℓⁿ) for fixed f > 1 prime to ℓ. Let C = Cl(L), let J be complex conjugation, and write E = (1 − J)C. The source supplies a bound B0 for the index of ℓC + (1 − γ)C, for its chosen Galois element γ. It also supplies N and n0, independent of n, such that in the integral group ring (γ − 1)N belongs to the ideal generated by θ, 1 + J and ℓ for n ≥ n0. Here θ is the integral element thetaH, whose coefficients use one representative from each pair of opposite residues. Stickelberger annihilation gives θ(1 − J)C = 0. The source selects the smoothing integer 2fℓ + 1. Uniform group-ring relation[795] Uniform index bound[796] Stickelberger annihilation[797] Choice of parameter and cyclotomic cases[798]

Put T = 1 − γ. Multiply the relation by 1 − J. The θ term kills the class group, the 1 + J term disappears because J² = 1, and the last term has image inside ℓE. Hence TN kills V = E/ℓE. Each quotient TaV/Ta+1V is an image of V/TV. The map 1 − J in turn sends C/(ℓC + TC) onto V/TV. Multiplying the at most N quotient sizes gives |V| ≤ B0N. On the finite group E, the kernel and cokernel of multiplication by ℓ have the same order, so the same bound holds for |E[ℓ]|. Group-ring relation acting on the class group[799] Bound for a nilpotent endomorphism[800]

At odd ℓ a reflection inequality bounds |C/(ℓC + E)| by ℓ times the number of ℓ-torsion elements on which conjugation acts by −1. Each such element x lies in E, since (1 − J)(((ℓ + 1)/2)x) = x, with the integer scalar (ℓ + 1)/2. The remaining factor |(ℓC + E)/ℓC| is at most |E/ℓE|. The resulting bound is ℓB02N. At ℓ = 2 put C− = ker(1 + J). The separate sign estimate gives [C−∶E] ≤ (2φ(4f))N, where φ is Euler’s totient. On C[2], the map 1 − J has image in E[2] and kernel in C−[2]. The latter has order at most [C−∶E] |E[2]|. The source uses the looser uniform bound ([C−∶E] |E[2]|)². Reflection at odd primes[801] Odd-prime index product[802] Sign estimate at 2[803] Two-primary index bound[804]

To transfer either bound, denoted by B, to the abelian field K, use its inclusion in a cyclotomic field. The embedding lemma chooses f,D before n. For every K′ = K(μℓⁿ) it produces a full cyclotomic field L of conductor fℓm, with m ≥ n0 and [L∶K′] ≤ Dℓn₀. Restrict the unramified ℤ/ℓ-characters from K′ to L. The size of the restriction kernel is bounded by the subgroup index [L∶K′], and Artin reciprocity bounds its image by the number of class-group characters of L. Thus |Cl(K′)/ℓCl(K′)| ≤ Dℓn₀B. The written proof chooses this integer itself for r, since it is at most ℓr. The arithmetic inputs to this derivation include the group-ring relation, the uniform ambiguous-class index, Stickelberger annihilation, reflection and the sign estimate at 2. Their statements have the pinned suppliers above. Embedding and degree calculation[805] Restriction of class-group characters[806] Uniform transfer[794]

8.6From class-group characters to generators

Let U∞ be the kernel of the ℓ-adic cyclotomic character on the absolute Galois group, and put A = ℚℓ/ℤℓ. For an integer s ≥ 1, let Ds be the group of locally constant homomorphisms U∞ → A vanishing on its intersections with every inertia group and with each decomposition group above a prime dividing s. Define Xs = Homℤℓ(Ds, A). The earlier cokernel calculation uses s = ℓ. The generator proof starts at s = 1. Local conditions on the characters[807] Definition of the character module[808] Its ℤℓ-linear dual[809]

At the finite field K(μℓⁿ), n ≥ 2, class field theory pulls the class-group characters onto the everywhere unramified ℤ/ℓ-characters. Their number is bounded by the cardinality of Cl/ℓCl, since they factor through that finite vector space and its dual has the same dimension. At infinite level every such character extends to a finite level. The extension theorem first extends the locally constant homomorphism and then enforces the local conditions after moving higher. Compactness of the relevant sets of decomposition and inertia elements makes a single higher level suffice. The images under restriction from successive levels are nested and cover the infinite-level characters. Any ℓr + 1 distinct characters would therefore already occur together at one level, contradicting the finite bound. Adding the decomposition conditions for s can only reduce their number. Class characters at each layer[810] Extending the character and its local conditions[811] Nested union at infinite level[812] Comparison of local conditions[813]

Every element of Ds has ℓ-power order. Its domain is compact, so its locally constant image is finite, and every element of A is killed by a power of ℓ. Further, Ds[ℓ] has at most ℓr elements by the character bound and the identification A[ℓ] ≅ ℤ/ℓ. Embed this vector space in Ar using at most r coordinates. Each coordinate extends to all of Ds because A is divisible and hence injective over the principal ideal domain ℤℓ. Their joint map is still injective. Indeed a nonzero kernel element of order ℓk would yield a nonzero kernel element of order ℓ by multiplication by ℓk−1. Any map Ds → A now extends to Ar. Each endomorphism of A is scalar multiplication by an ℓ-adic integer, as seen by its compatible values on the cyclic groups A[ℓk]. The r extended coordinates thus generate Xs. This proves the precise generator conclusion used in the layer bound, a surjection ℤℓr → Xs. Torsion of the character module[814] Embedding from its order-ℓ subgroup[815] Producing the generators of the dual[816] Endomorphisms of ℚℓ/ℤℓ[817]

8.7One generator bound before choosing the two primes

At each odd ℓ the abelian field datum is fixed. The argument above works in any realization of that field and the source takes R = max(1, r) to meet the positivity hypothesis. At 2 the field varies with q,d. Fix the abelian base datum M of degree b, adjoin i with i² = −1, and obtain an exponent g from the class-group bound there. Adjoining the two quadratic fields specified by q and d gives a generator bound uniform in all prime pairs with q ≡ 3 mod 8, d ≡ 7 mod 16 and qd coprime to the modulus of M. Transport between field realizations[818] Fixed odd-prime bound[819] Quantifiers for the varying fields at 2[820]

R2 = 4(g + 6b).

Allow ramification at q and then at d in the larger space of mod-2 characters. Their inertia groups can be tested on at most 2b and 4b orbits respectively, by the two congruences. Evaluating on one tame inertia generator per representative gives at most two choices per orbit. Two characters with the same values differ by one from the previous space. Thus the character count is at most 2g+6b. Next pass to the subgroups corresponding to the two quadratic extensions. Each step at most squares the count. For an index-two subgroup, conjugation by an outside element induces an involution c on its characters. In characteristic 2, (1 + c)² = 0, so the image lies in its kernel, the invariant characters. The source bounds the number of invariants by the old character count. Evaluation on the square of the outside element records the obstruction to extending an invariant character, and the quotient character of the index-two subgroup records this bit after extension. Hence the number of all characters is at most the square of the old count. Two squarings give the displayed exponent. Restoring the unramified and splitting conditions selects a subgroup, so the same bound applies to the two tower modules X1 and X2. Orbit counts from the prime congruences[821] Testing on tame inertia[822] The invariant characters and the extension obstruction[823] Index-two bound[824] Two local steps and two squarings[825]

8.8Why restriction recovers the locally trivial classes

Fix a field F in one of these towers. Let G be its absolute Galois group, χ its cyclotomic character, U = ker χ, and e a nonzero integer. The coefficient module A = ℚℓ/ℤℓ carries the action ρ(g) = χ(g)−e. For a class in degree one, inflate to G and restrict a cocycle z to U. Since U acts trivially, z restricts to an additive character φ, and every coboundary restricts to zero. Conjugation of the cocycle identity gives φ(gug−1) = ρ(g)φ(u). Local triviality forces φ to vanish on inertia and on decomposition groups above ℓ, in each case after intersection with U. We will recover exactly the equivariant characters with these vanishing conditions. Transport of the infinite character group and its fixed-point condition[826] Image of the locally trivial subgroup[827]

For injectivity, suppose φ = 0. The cocycle then factors through the cyclotomic quotient. In our fields this quotient is procyclic. Choose g whose image topologically generates it. The value χ(g)−e − 1 is nonzero. Indeed the cyclotomic degrees over a fixed number field grow without bound, whereas the ℓ-adic roots of a fixed nonzero power are finite. Multiplication by this nonzero scalar is surjective on A, so choose a with (ρ(g) − 1)a = z(g). Subtract its coboundary. The resulting cocycle vanishes on g, hence by the cocycle rule on all its powers, and by continuity on the quotient. This is where the condition e ≠ 0 enters. Injectivity and the nontrivial cyclotomic power[828]

For surjectivity let φ be one of the equivariant characters. Write C for the closure of the powers of a lift of a cyclotomic generator. Its compact image surjects onto χ(G), so G = CU. The source proves that φ vanishes on C ∩ U. In group-theoretic terms the pro-ℓ part of the procyclic group C maps onto an infinite pro-ℓ group. That part is ℤℓ, and all its nonzero closed subgroups have finite index. Its kernel is therefore zero. The intersection has only prime-to-ℓ finite quotients, so its continuous characters into ℓ-primary torsion vanish. The code proves this vanishing directly by congruences in finite quotients. We may consequently define

z(cu) = ρ(c)φ(u),   c ∈ C,   u ∈ U.

Two decompositions differ by an element of the intersection, making the formula independent of the choice. Equivariance gives the cocycle identity on multiplying two decompositions. Continuity follows because C × U → G is a continuous surjection of compact Hausdorff spaces, hence a quotient map. Away from ℓ, inertia already lies in the cyclotomic kernel, where φ vanishes. Above ℓ, the restricted cocycle vanishes on the kernel of the local cyclotomic character. Its image on the decomposition group is open in ℤℓ×, and the allowed roots of unity give the same procyclic condition. The preceding generator argument therefore subtracts a local coboundary. Inflation from the group unramified outside ℓ now supplies a locally trivial class, whose restriction is φ. Vanishing on the intersection[829] Extension to a continuous cocycle[830] Local coboundary at places above ℓ[831] Local conditions and descent from the absolute group[827]

8.9The inverse action and the Tate twist

Return to the base field L0 and one of its cyclotomic layers Lm of relative degree ℓm, embedded in the same algebraic closure. The two fields have the same infinite cyclotomic kernel. Write c for the largest exponent such that L0 contains a primitive ℓcth root. Under the roots-of-unity hypothesis its cyclotomic image is 1 + ℓcℤℓ. The subgroup for the layer has image 1 + ℓc+mℤℓ. Choose γ in the base Galois group lifting a generator of its cyclotomic image. The valuation of χ(γ) − 1 is exactly c, and b = γℓm generates the image for that layer. In these statements “generator” refers to the closure of powers in the cyclotomic image. On the common character module D = Dℓ the action is (de(g)φ)(u) = χ(g)−eφ(g−1ug). Equivariance says that φ is fixed by the layer group. It suffices to require it fixed by b, equivalently by b−1. Indeed each character is killed by a power of ℓ and its conjugation action is locally constant on a sufficiently high congruence subgroup. Powers of χ(b) meet every needed open coset. Thus the kernel of de(b−1) − 1 is the entire invariant group just identified with Sha. The linear dual X = Homℤℓ(D, A) carries the contragredient action xe(g)f = f ∘ de(g−1). Consequently its scalar factor is χ(g)+e. Put T = de(b−1) − 1. Restriction X → Hom(ker T, A) is onto by injectivity of A. Its kernel consists exactly of the maps f ∘ T. Indeed a functional vanishing on ker T factors through the image of T and extends from there to D. This identifies the dual of ker T with the cokernel of xe(b) − 1. Duality with A preserves length. For finite length, dualize a composition series and use that the dual of ℤ/ℓ is again ℤ/ℓ. For infinite length, annihilators reverse strict inclusions of submodules since A separates points of their quotients. Arbitrarily long chains therefore persist in the dual. length Sha¹(Lm, A(−e)) = length [X / ((χ(γ)ex0(γ))ℓm − 1)X].

Here x0 denotes the untwisted dual action. The equality holds for each nonzero integer e and takes values in the extended natural numbers. The window uses e ≥ 1.

As an algebraic check of the signs, take ℓ = 3, D = ℚ3/ℤ3, χ(γ) = 4, and let the untwisted action on D be multiplication by 4 at γ. The untwisted dual action on X = ℤ3 is multiplication by 1/4. For e = 1 the two twisted actions at γ are the identity. At layer zero the whole character group is fixed and the dual cokernel is all of ℤ3, both of infinite length. Using a negative scalar exponent on the dual would instead give 1/16 − 1 = −15/16, which has 3-adic valuation 1. This example tests the algebra underlying the formula. The arithmetic window supplies its own finiteness estimates.

At the reference layer the proof also needs a comparison with degree two. The Tate dual of A(−e) has integral coefficient twist e + 1. Under finite-level Poitou–Tate duality, local finiteness and local Tate duality, the two locally trivial groups have equal length. The source uses a decreasing filtration on the locally trivial degree-two group and an increasing torsion-level filtration on degree one. The former is separated and the latter exhaustive. At all sufficiently high levels the finite quotients of the first and the finite pieces of the second have equal cardinality by finite-level duality and control of localization. Their lengths therefore agree, including the case of unbounded lengths. The degree-two group embeds into full H², giving the upper bound used for the exceptional twists. g = ueγ,   hm(e) = lengthℤℓ X / (gℓm − 1)X,

To prove the inequality, reduce X modulo ℓ. The quotient is a vector space of dimension at most R over the field with ℓ elements. On it, g − 1 equals γ − 1 and is nilpotent. Its successive images must strictly decrease in dimension until they vanish, so its Rth power vanishes. Put k = ⌊logℓ R⌋ + 1. Since ℓk ≥ R, the characteristic-ℓ binomial identity gives gℓk ≡ 1 modulo ℓ. For any w ≡ 1 modulo ℓ, the sum S = 1 + w + ⋯ + wℓ−1 maps X into ℓX. Now take w ≡ 1 modulo ℓ². For each x, Sx ≡ ℓx modulo ℓ²X. Thus SX ⊆ ℓX and ℓX = SX + ℓ(ℓX). The quotient ℓX/SX is finitely generated and equals its own multiple by the maximal ideal (ℓ). Nakayama’s lemma makes it zero. Hence the cokernel of S has length at most R. For endomorphisms A,B, the sequence coker B → coker(AB) → coker A → 0 is exact, with first map induced by A. For m below j0, the larger power minus one factors through the smaller, so the smaller-layer quotient has no greater length. This argument also holds for lengths taking the value ∞. hm(e) ≤ ∑i=1R [max(m, j0) + c + vℓ(si − e)].

Two integers in the same such ball differ by a multiple of ℓB+1, while their ordinary distance is less than Z < ℓB+1. They coincide. At most R twists are marked. On the others each valuation vℓ(si − e) is at most B, giving a finite bound at once. Separation of two integer twists[861] Exceptional set independent of the layer[862]

For every unmarked e in [1, Z],   hm(e) ≤ R(max(m, j0) + c + ⌊logℓ Z⌋).

For a marked twist use the other estimate. Poitou–Tate duality and the local finiteness and duality hypotheses identify the degree-one length at j0 with that of a locally trivial degree-two group. The latter embeds into the full degree-two cohomology with coefficients ℤℓ(e + 1). The full group’s length VLen therefore bounds hj₀(e). The growth inequality carries this bound to every m. The independent estimate LemmaK gives finiteness of that full group and bounds the logarithm of its order by exp((2en)CK log(2D)), where n is the field degree over ℚ and D its absolute discriminant. 8.12Why finitely many marked twists leave a whole interval

Fix the outer scale X and combine the dyadic marks with the marks for the fixed collection of odd primes. The union has size at most R, fixed before choosing X. Put α = ε/(2CK) and β = Ct, so 0 < α ≤ β. A marked integer e is troublesome only when xα < e ≤ xβ. Above this range it is absent from the sum. Below it we can use the degree-two estimate, since eCK ≤ xε/2. The field degree and discriminant in that estimate still have to be bounded.

Write u = log x, a = (log e)/β and B = β/α. This mark forbids exactly a ≤ u < Ba. A window [Y, Y²] becomes [y, 2y] in this coordinate. Begin with an upper limit U = log X. If each mark satisfies a ≤ U/(2B) or a > U, the entire top interval [U/2, U] is safe. Otherwise choose a mark with U/(2B) < a ≤ U. Lower the upper limit to U/(2B). This mark now lies strictly beyond it, so remove that mark and repeat. In at most R reductions the process stops. Thus one may use the source’s conservative uniform constant J = 2R+2BR, with X1/J ≤ Y and Y² ≤ X. Every marked twist still in the sum is small enough throughout the same interval. In the preceding window argument, a marked twist can approach an ℓ-adic root too closely for its valuation to give a uniform estimate. The proof returns to a finite layer, where it bounds a different quantity. Let ℓ be any prime and L a totally complex number field of degree n and absolute discriminant Δ. Assume L contains a primitive ℓth root of unity for odd ℓ, or a primitive fourth root when ℓ = 2. Let S be all finite primes over ℓ and GS the Galois group unramified outside them. The assertion holds for every algebraic closure, every choice of places above S and every compatible descended cyclotomic character.

For every integer e ≥ 1,   H²(GS, ℤℓ(e + 1)) is finite,   log |H²| ≤ KC(e,n,Δ) = exp((2en)C log(2Δ)).

One exponent works simultaneously for all these choices. Tracing three numerical witnesses in the proof gives C = 150. The theorem returned to the window argument quantifies existentially over C. The numerical estimate applies to log order, so a length bound is obtained by dividing by log ℓ. d ≤ (n + 1)(4e + 4),   ℓc ≤ 2n′,   Δ′ ≤ Δd(ℓc)n′,   s(L) ≤ s(L′).

The relative different contains N, hence its norm divides Nn′. The tower discriminant formula and N ≤ ℓc give the displayed estimate. The independent Selmer count bounds |EqHom| qr₂ by BℓX. Its ℓ-primary kernel estimate uses the identity vℓ(aℓν−c − 1) = ν + vℓ(e). At ℓ = 2 the primitive-fourth-root hypothesis ensures c ≥ 2. |EqHom| ≤ T2eT2e+1 ℓX,   X = (b + f)g + c + f.

The right side is independent of ν. To see why this matters, take any finite set of distinct locally trivial classes. Restriction to the infinite cyclotomic level is injective. Each restricted class can be represented at a sufficiently high finite level and killed there by ℓν. A common level works for the whole finite set. Thus s(L′) is finite and ℓs(L′) satisfies the same upper bound. We can now construct the functional Φ used above. Its scalar part takes one input from each of the e pairs in the cyclic word and one from the gluing element. Let k be the finite residue field, let ζ have order q in k×, put r = |k×|/q and fix the additive index v on k× with values in ℤ/q. u(a,b) = [L(a) + L(b) − L(ab)] / (qr).

This integer is symmetric in its arguments. Compute the sum of the carries for a product of three elements by putting the parentheses on either side. The intermediate logarithm cancels, giving u(a,b) + u(ab,c) = u(b,c) + u(a,bc). Reduce modulo q. On a word of length 2e + 1 take the product of u over its first e consecutive pairs, times v of the last entry. This is a cocycle, a functional vanishing on boundaries. For a weight x let χ(j) = ζxj. Sum one carry u(χ(j),χ(1)) over j modulo q. The sums of L(χ(j)) and L(χ(j + 1)) agree by a cyclic shift. The result is L(χ(1))/r ≡ x modulo q. In the first two cases a matrix outside E moves the distinguished line to a different line. Row additions preserving the first line can take that new line to a fixed second coordinate line. Thus all such matrices form one double coset of E. Transposing gives the same result for the distinguished hyperplane in the third case. At any one vertex, the proof passes to the finite group G = Kᵣ/core(B), where core(B) is the intersection of all Kᵣ-conjugates of B. Use the same letters for subgroup images. It equals ‖f‖² on E. Elsewhere it is constant because it depends only on the double coset. Its mean over s is zero, so its value outside E is nonpositive. |⟨f,g⟩| = |⟨P′f,g⟩| ≤ ‖f‖‖g‖ / √[E′:B].

At vertex 0, the matrices I + t e₁₀ in E₀₂ move the line to span(e₀ + t e₁) inside the same plane. Distinct t modulo π give distinct flags, so [E₀₂:B] ≥ q. Likewise I + t e₂₁ in E₀₁ sends e₁ to e₁ + t e₂ while fixing e₀. This supplies [E₀₁:B] ≥ q, the other needed index. Thus every pairing has coefficient at most 1/√q ≤ 1/5. A calculation at the threshold. In size N = 3 over 𝔽₂₅, the graph at vertex 0 joins points to lines in the projective plane. There are (25³ − 1)/(25 − 1) = 651 points and as many lines. Each line contains 26 points. Give one point value +1, a second point value −1, and all other points zero. Averaging on each line gives +1/26 on the 25 lines through just the first point, −1/26 on the 25 through just the second, and zero elsewhere. The common line cancels. The ratio of output norm to input norm is √(50/26²)/√2 = 5/26. In fact this is the norm on the entire mean-zero subspace. If A is the line-by-point incidence matrix, ATA has diagonal entries 26 and off-diagonal entries 1, since two points determine one line. It acts by 25 on vectors with zero sum. The averaging matrix is A/26. Here the general bound 1/√26 and its uniform relaxation 1/5 both exceed the exact value 5/26. How the three local bounds of 1/5 give a gap of 3/5

Work in the real Hilbert space of square-integrable coefficients on the common cover. Let Pᵢ project orthogonally onto the three closed spaces of invariant coefficients just used. Write Qᵢ = I − Pᵢ for the part lost in this projection. Start with a pair of spaces, and remove from x its projection onto their common subspace. Call the result z. This removal leaves both Qᵢx and Qⱼx unchanged. Write a = Pᵢz, b = Pⱼz and S = ‖a‖² + ‖b‖². The flag estimate gives 2⟨a,b⟩ ≤ S/5. Since S = ⟨z,a + b⟩, Cauchy–Schwarz gives S² ≤ ‖z‖² · (6/5)S. Thus the sum of the two squared losses, T = 2‖z‖² − S, is at least (4/5)‖z‖². From the incidence angle to two projection losses[1030]

Set rᵢ = Qᵢx. For the pair, ⟨rᵢ + rⱼ,z⟩ = T. A second application of Cauchy–Schwarz gives ‖rᵢ + rⱼ‖² ≥ (4/5)T, including the zero case. Sum over all three pairs. Every individual ‖rᵢ‖² occurs twice on the right. On the left the sum of pair squares is ‖∑rᵢ‖² + ∑‖rᵢ‖². Subtraction leaves the factor 2 · (4/5) − 1 = 3/5. To put the bound on the original coefficient, write E(x) = ⟨Dx,x⟩ = ∑‖Qᵢx‖². Cauchy–Schwarz for the positive form ⟨D·,·⟩ gives ‖Dx‖⁴ ≤ E(x)E(Dx). The preceding estimate now implies E(y) ≥ (3/5)‖y‖² for every y in the range of D. The operator is self-adjoint, and its kernel consists of the vectors fixed by all three projections. Its range is dense in the orthogonal complement of that kernel. Continuity therefore gives the same gap on the whole complement. This is the inequality used in the next calculation. |EqHom| qr₂ ≤ B ℓX,   X = (b + f)g + c + f.

How an integral boundary matrix bounds torsion

The character count above uses the orders of the torsion subgroups of two integral homology groups. A torsion class is killed by a nonzero integer. An infinite free summand in homology can therefore coexist with the finite quantity we need to bound. Start with a free lattice E = ℤr, with r ≤ A, and any set of integral relation vectors. Write Λ for their integer span. Suppose each relation has sum of absolute coordinates at most b, where b ≥ 1. The bound used in the proof is

|tors(E/Λ)| ≤ bA.

If we have r independent relation vectors, put them in a square matrix V. The sublattice they generate has index |det V|. Expanding the determinant as a signed sum over permutations and taking absolute values gives a sum of products. Allowing every choice of one column for each row only increases this sum, and the enlarged sum factors as ∏i ∑j |Vij|. This proves the bound br. Additional relations give a quotient of this finite group. Permutation expansion and row sums[1079] Lattice index from the determinant[1080]

Suppose instead that the relation vectors span only a proper rational subspace. Choose a maximal independent subset and complete it to a rational basis using standard unit vectors. Let K be the integer span of that completed list. Its determinant still has absolute value at most br, since every added vector has length one. To compare torsion, choose a lift in E for each torsion class in E/Λ and reduce its lift modulo K. If two images coincide, the difference x of their lifts lies in K. Their difference class is torsion, so some nonzero multiple of x belongs to Λ. Consequently x lies in the rational span of the original relations. In the completed basis every coefficient of an added vector must then vanish. Because x belongs to K, the remaining coefficients are integers. Thus x is an integer combination of selected relations and the two classes were equal. This injects the set of torsion classes into the finite set E/K. For example, impose the three relations (2,0,0), (0,2,0), (1,1,0) in ℤ³. The third coordinate stays free. In the first two coordinates a vector is a relation exactly when the coordinates have the same parity. Hence the torsion subgroup has order two. Choosing the first two relations and the third unit vector gives det V = 4. The general bound gives 2³ = 8. The three numbers measure respectively the actual torsion, the index for this completed list, and the estimate using the common row bound.

The extra cost in positive homological degree

Let a group G permute the simplex basis in each degree and commute with each face map. Suppose the augmented complex is exact through degree m. An orbit identifies simplices related by the action. A stabilizer fixes a specified simplex. Suppose there are at most A orbits per degree up to m and every corresponding stabilizer has order at most s ≥ 1. A boundary in degree m + 1 is an alternating sum of m + 2 faces. After identifying generators in the same orbit, coordinates add and the sum of their absolute values can only decrease. In degree zero the coefficient module at the end of the induction is generally a kernel. Identifying g x with x presents the coinvariants of that module. It gives the determinant factor (m + 2)A. For positive degree, take the short exact sequence given by the first permutation module, its augmentation and its kernel. The long exact homology sequence compares the desired torsion with the torsion one degree lower for that kernel and the finite homology of the permutation module. For a single orbit the latter is the homology of the stabilizer by Shapiro’s lemma. A group of order h has hj bar generators in degree j > 0, and multiplication by h kills its homology. The cycles form a subgroup of a free abelian group with that many generators, hence the homology has order at most hhʲ. Combining the orbits costs at most sA sʲ. Repeating the exact-sequence comparison for j = m, …, 1 gives

|tors Hm(G,ℤ)| ≤ (m + 2)A sm A sᵐ.

The last exponent uses ∑j=1m sj ≤ m sm. This part needs the orbit and stabilizer estimates, exactness of the complex, the long exact sequence, Shapiro’s lemma and annihilation of finite-group homology. Each supplies a distinct input. How many faces can an arithmetic group have up to symmetry?

In the homology inequality, A bounds the number of face orbits and s bounds the order of the subgroup fixing any one face. A face in this chain model is an ordered tuple of vertices, with repetitions allowed. Two such tuples represent one orbit if the same group element moves every entry of the first tuple to the corresponding entry of the second. Here the group is G = GLN(𝒪F), with F a totally complex number field, n = [F : ℚ], D = |disc F|, N ≥ 1 and d = nN. Thus d is the integer rank of the vector lattice 𝒪FN. We will count orbits in each face degree p ≥ 0. The two inputs to the homology theorem[1092]

Find a frame shared by the whole face

For each infinite place of F take a Hermitian form on ℂN. Their values on the images of a lattice vector y add to a real number qh(y). Impose qh(y) ≥ 1 for every nonzero y. A vector is minimal for h when equality holds. A vertex is a feasible family h uniquely determined by its equalities. A degree-p face in the complex is an ordered list of p + 1 such vertices at which one supporting linear functional attains its minimum. That functional is strictly positive on nonzero positive semidefinite families. The definition allows repeated vertices. Lattice evaluations and inequalities[1093] vertices and their common minimizing functional[1094] the ordered faces and group action[1095]

The common minimal vectors of a face span FN. To see why, average the vertices. At the average a lattice inequality is tight exactly when it is tight at every vertex. If the common minimal vectors missed a direction, a nonzero F-linear functional λ would vanish on their span. The family of rank-one forms obtained from |λ|² at all embeddings is positive semidefinite and nonzero. A sufficiently small subtraction of this family from the average preserves the tight constraints. Local finiteness of the inequalities keeps the others feasible. The supporting functional would strictly decrease below its minimum. Thus we can choose N independent common minimal columns and place them in a matrix A. They form a basis over F. Its integral determinant can be a nonunit. The determinant estimate gives

r = |NormF/ℚ(det A)| ≤ J,   J = DNdd.

For this last inequality the source pulls each local form back by A. The pulled-back determinants have product at most one by the diagonal bounds and Hadamard’s inequality. Their product is r times the product of the original determinants, for which the geometric lower bound is 1/J. One congruence count for the frame

Fix its positive integer r. Over F put B = rA−1. Why does this have integral entries? The principal ideal (det A) has norm r and contains the integer r. Hence r/det A lies in 𝒪F, and multiplying the integral adjugate of A by that element gives B. Reduce its entries modulo r𝒪F. Suppose a second frame A′ has the same norm and its matrix B′ has the same residue list. Write B − B′ = rX with X integral. Over the field this gives

A′A−1 = 1 + A′X,   AA′−1 = 1 − AX.

Both matrices are integral and they are inverses. The first therefore belongs to G and takes A to A′ by left multiplication. An integral basis identifies 𝒪F/r𝒪F as an additive group with (ℤ/rℤ)n. The list of N² entries has at most rnN² = rdN values. Choosing one frame for each attained list covers every orbit. Summing the bound for r = 1,…,J costs at most J1+dN. Example. In ℤ[i] take the one-column matrices A = 1 + i and A′ = 1 − i. Both norms are 2. The scaled inverses are B = 1 − i and B′ = 1 + i, so X = −i. The formula gives g = −i, and multiplication by this Gaussian unit sends 1 + i to 1 − i. This tests the congruence argument for frames of bounded determinant norm.

How many vertices can share a chosen frame?

Fix a representative A. A nearby vector is one that can be minimal for some feasible form making every column of A minimal. The coordinate estimate gives |σ((By)j)| ≤ R = NNJ² at every embedding. Since AB = r·1, the vector By determines y. Each of its coordinates has at most (2R + 1)n possibilities. Indeed, if two such algebraic integers differ by (2R + 1)x, every conjugate of x has absolute value at most 2R/(2R + 1) < 1. A nonzero algebraic integer has nonzero integer norm, ruling this out. The residue count thus bounds the number of nearby vectors by M = (2R + 1)d. The coordinate estimate on the scaled inverse[1104] separation by conjugate size[1105] counting all coordinates[1106]

The equations qh(y) = 1 are linear in the unknown coefficients of h. At a vertex, at most dN independent equations suffice to determine it. Their vectors lie in the nearby set. A set of at most dN vectors drawn from M choices can be recorded as a list of length dN by sorting it and padding with a blank. Hence this frame admits at most (M + 1)dN vertices. Each entry of an ordered tuple can use any of these in an upper bound. Together with the frame count this gives the orbit bound

Ap = J1+dN(M + 1)dN(p+1) ≤ (2Dd)12(p+1)d³N.

This count allows lists that fail the common-support condition, which only enlarges the bound. Formally choose a frame and a translated tuple for each orbit. Equal choices of frame and entries give the same tuple, hence the same orbit. Why reduction modulo three counts stabilizers

An element fixing an ordered tuple fixes its first vertex. The first vertex has finitely many minimal vectors, and these include N independent ones. The images of those basis vectors under an element fixing the vertex are again minimal and determine the element. Thus the stabilizer is finite. Now view it as a subgroup of the units of the matrix ring T = MN(𝒪F). Distinct elements have distinct residues in T/3T. Otherwise their quotient would be a finite-order unit congruent to 1 modulo 3. Finiteness from minimal vectors[1111] modulo-three separation[1112]

Here is the divisibility argument behind this separation. If such a unit were nontrivial, one of its powers would have prime order l and still be congruent to 1. Write that power as 1 + 3kY with k ≥ 1 maximal and Y nonzero modulo 3. Maximality follows by looking at any nonzero integer coordinate in the free abelian group T. For l ≠ 3 its lth power differs from 1 by l3kY modulo 3k+1, which is nonzero. For l = 3 the leading term is 3k+1Y modulo 3k+2. The other two terms in the cube are divisible by 32k+1 and 33k, both at least the required power. This contradicts prime order in both cases. The source proves the same separation by induction on the order. The power divisible by three[1113] the prime-to-three power[1114]

The additive rank of T is nN² = dN, so the stabilizer bound is s = 3dN, uniform in the face degree. In rank one over ℤ[i] the units 1, −1, i, −i already have four distinct residues among the nine available. In homology degree m, Am bounds every face degree p ≤ m. How multiplication modulo the level produces a Bernoulli value

The length argument needs an integer-like scalar whose ℓ-adic valuation is exactly that of a special value. The floor in its definition records the carry when an integer product is reduced modulo the level. This permits a direct comparison of the two quantities, one residue at a time. For a unit residue, write u for its representative in 1,…,F−1. Choose b prime to F and divide bu by F, obtaining a quotient j and a remainder y between 1 and F−1. The opposite residue is represented by F−u. Its product with b is (b−j−1)F + (F−y). Subtracting the two quotients gives the signed carry θ(u) = 2j − (b−1). Define S = ∑u θ(u)ueχ(u), summed over the unit representatives. The use of ue in place of a lifted cyclotomic character changes the scalar by a multiple of ℓm. C(u) = uk/(kF) − uk−1/2 + (2F/D)nu,   nu ∈ ℤ.

Indeed the term of Bernoulli index h ≥ 2 has a factor Fh−1. The denominator bound for the Bernoulli number Bh says that PBh is an integer for h ≤ k. To keep track of the remainder, expand yk modulo F² and ye modulo F. Multiplication by D clears every denominator in the remainder, with one factor F left. Which character takes values in the cyclotomic integers?

The Jacobi identity multiplies two algebraic integers. A sum computed only modulo p would lose the ideal it is supposed to measure. The algebraic integer ζ satisfies the cyclotomic polynomial ΦM. Its reduction satisfies the same polynomial modulo p. Lift the residue 2 at level five

Take M = 5 and p = 11, with πζ = 3. The powers of 3 starting at exponent zero are 1, 3, 9, 5, 4 and then 1. Since h = 2, square the input 2 to obtain 4. The required lift is χ(2) = ζ⁴. Squaring this value gives χ(4) = ζ³. Checking the other way, 4² ≡ 5 ≡ 3³ modulo 11. For the other reduction π′ζ = 9, the input 2 still gives 2² = 4. Since 9² ≡ 4 modulo 11, its lift is now χ′(2) = ζ². The prime ideal is part of the construction.

Why every prime above p occurs only once

For each invertible residue t modulo M let σt(ζ) = ζt and put Pt = ker(π ∘ σt). This inverse-image convention is what sets the indices in the signed divisor. Every reduction is onto, since ordinary integers already give all of 𝔽p. Its kernel is therefore a maximal ideal of norm p. If two kernels agreed, subtract from any algebraic integer the ordinary integer representing its first reduction. The difference would also belong to the second kernel, forcing both reductions to agree on that element. Applying this to ζ gives (πζ)s = (πζ)t, hence s = t. These φ(M) distinct maximal ideals are pairwise coprime, and each divides (p). Their product divides (p) and already has norm pφ(M). This equals the norm of (p), because [K : ℚ] = φ(M). The leftover integral ideal has norm one and is the unit ideal. Thus (p) = ∏tPt. For a Jacobi sum J dividing p, this gives ordPₜ(J) ∈ {0,1}. Testing π(σtJ) = 0 tells exactly which exponent is one. In the example at 11 the four reductions send ζ to 3, 9, 5 and 4. A repeated prime would exhaust too much of the norm. To tell which primes occur, reduce σt(Jj) modulo P. The result is ∑ xA(1 − x)B with A = h[t]N and B = h[jt]N. Both exponents lie strictly between 0 and p − 1. Expand the binomial. In degree A + k the sum of powers over the field vanishes unless p − 1 divides the degree. Since all degrees are positive and below 2(p − 1), only k = p − 1 − A can contribute. When this index is in the expansion its binomial coefficient is nonzero modulo p, since B < p. Thus the residue is zero exactly when A + B < p − 1, or [t]N + [jt]N < N. The remaining indices give B₀ = 1, B₁ = −½ and Bh = 0 for odd h > 1. Thus PkBh is integral throughout, and fPk times the displayed coefficient is an integer, residue by residue. 9The one-sided window theorem

Suppose the arithmetic argument repeatedly finds a stretch of scales on which a centered prime sum stays below a small power of the scale. A zero of an associated L-function would force a pole of its transform. How can a bound on scattered stretches rule out even one pole? High derivatives let us choose where the integral sees the function.

9.1The hypothesis in logarithmic coordinates

Fix 0 < θ < 1 and δ > 0. Write g(u) = GF(exp u) for a real weighted sum from a finite character family F. The abstract theorem below allows any real measurable g with |g(u)| ≤ C0 exp(2u) for u ≥ 0. Its transform Φ(s) agrees with ∫0∞ g(u) exp(−su) du for Re s > 2. Assume it extends holomorphically in the right half-plane outside a set Z of simple poles, every one of which has positive real part. Every point of the half-plane must have a punctured neighborhood free of Z, including points outside Z. At each pole the residue is nonzero, and at each real pole it is real and strictly positive. These assumptions comprise PoleData. Transform and pole hypotheses[1463]

Put U = log Y. Then [Y, Y1+δ] becomes I = [U, (1 + δ)U]. For every η > 0 and every lower limit U0, suppose there exist U ≥ U0 and a majorant R on I with R ≥ max(g, 0), such that R(u) exp(−θu) is integrable there and

∫I R(u) exp(−θu) du ≤ exp(ηU).

Theorem. Every ρ ∈ Z satisfies Re ρ ≤ θ. The window and its majorant may depend on η and U0. Between windows the growth estimate still holds. An arithmetic upper bound GF(y) ≤ C yθ on arbitrarily distant windows suffices. Take R(u) = |C| exp(θu). Its weighted integral equals |C|δU, which is at most exp(ηU) once U is large. From power bounds to the window hypothesis[1464] One-sided window theorem[1465]

Test the hypothesis on a single pole. Take θ = ½, δ = ½ and g(u) = exp(¾u). Its Laplace transform is 1/(s − ¾). On [U,3U/2] even the smallest admissible majorant has weighted integral 4(exp(3U/8) − exp(U/4)). For η = ⅛ this eventually exceeds exp(ηU) on every window. Change the sign of g and R = 0 works on every window, although the transform still has a pole at ¾. Its residue is now −1. This example explains the sign hypothesis at real poles and why the arithmetic only needs an upper bound.

9.2Choosing a derivative that sees the window

For Re z = σ > 2, define Ak(z) = (−1)kΦ(k)(z)/k!. In a small neighborhood with Re z ≥ 2 + α, α > 0, the differentiated integrand is bounded by C0uk exp(−αu), an integrable function. Repeated differentiation under the integral therefore gives

Ak(σ + iγ) = ∫0∞ g(u) exp(−iγu) Kk,σ(u) du,   Kk,a(u) = ukexp(−au)/k!.

This nonnegative kernel has its maximum at u = k/a for k > 0. Its integral is a−k−1, by substitution and integration by parts. The term g itself may change sign. Adding Re Ak(σ) to the triangle inequality for |Ak(σ + iγ)| replaces |g| by |g| + g = 2 max(g, 0). On I, use this majorant and the inequality vk/k! ≤ exp(v) at v = (σ − θ)u. Off I, use the growth bound. The result is

|Ak(σ + iγ)| + Re Ak(σ) ≤ 2 exp(ηU)/(σ − θ)k + 2C0 ∫(0,∞) ∖ I Kk,σ−2(u) du.

The real derivative acts as a correction for sign. Write g = g+ − g−, both parts nonnegative. The triangle inequality at σ + iγ counts both with a plus sign. At the real center, Ak(σ) = ∫(g+ − g−)K. Adding cancels the entire negative part and leaves at most 2∫g+K. The same derivative order must therefore work at both centers.

The integrand in this tail contains σ − 2 because |g| can grow as exp(2u). Estimating the tails of Kk,σ alone would lose that factor. Derivative identity[1466] One-sided derivative estimate[1467]

9.3A uniform estimate for the tails

For s > λ ≥ 0 and V = (1 + δ)U, multiply the integrand on u > V by exp(λ(u − V)), and on u < U by exp(λ(U − u)). Both multipliers are at least one in their respective regions. Extending the resulting integrals over the positive half-line gives

∫(0,∞) ∖ I Kk,s ≤ exp(−λV)/(s − λ)k+1 + exp(λU)/(s + λ)k+1.

The source makes concrete choices depending first on δ and then on the window. Take λ = 2 + 6/δ, M = λ(1 + δ), σ = M(2 + λ), s = σ − 2, and k = ⌈(1 + δ/2)σU⌉. For U ≥ 1 we have k ≥ U and s > λ. To bound the first term after multiplication by σk, set a = s − λ. The inequality log(σ/a) ≤ (σ − a)/a = 1/(M − 1), together with (1 + δ/2)σ = M(M − 1), gives −λV + k log(σ/a) ≤ 1. Its contribution is at most exp(1)/a.

For the second term set b = s + λ. Then log(σ/b) ≤ −(λ − 2)/b. Since (1 + δ/2)(λ − 2) = λ + 1 and λ(σ − 2 + λ) ≤ (λ + 1)σ, the lower bound on k gives λU − k(λ − 2)/b ≤ 0. Therefore this contribution is at most 1/b. Both bounds are independent of the chosen window. Combining with the preceding inequality gives a constant C1 such that, for every η > 0 and arbitrarily large U, some integer k ≥ U satisfies simultaneously for every real γ

Locate one of the kernels numerically

|Ak(σ + iγ)| + Re Ak(σ) ≤ C1 exp(ηU)/(σ − θ)k.

9.4Isolating the pole seen by the derivatives

Suppose a pole has real part greater than θ. All poles lie to the left of σ because the Laplace integral is holomorphic on Re s > 2. Write E = σ − θ. The closed disk of radius E about σ lies in Re s ≥ θ > 0, so it contains finitely many poles by compactness and the punctured-neighborhood assumption. If it contains no poles, take D = E. The hypothesized pole then has horizontal distance strictly less than D and gives the first case below. Otherwise let D be the distance from σ to a nearest pole in the disk. In both cases the open disk of radius D is pole-free.

If a pole ρ1 has σ − Re ρ1 < D, then a disk of radius D centered at σ + i Im ρ1 contains it. Move that center by a sufficiently small vertical amount. Only finitely many poles in a slightly enlarged disk matter, and two distinct poles equally far from the moving center can tie at at most one height. Indeed their squared distances have a difference affine in the height. For equal imaginary parts the equality would also require equal real parts, since both poles lie to the left of σ. Avoiding the finitely many ties gives a center z = σ + iγ with a unique nearest pole ρ at distance d < D. Choose a radius r with d < r ≤ D isolating this pole.

In the other case all horizontal distances σ − Re ρ are at least D. There must be a nearest pole in the disk because the hypothesized pole has horizontal distance less than E. For any nearest pole the Euclidean distance D is at least its horizontal distance, now at least D. Equality forces the imaginary part to vanish. This identifies one real pole β = σ − D > θ. Every other pole in the finite disk is strictly farther away. Choose r with D < r ≤ E isolating β. Geometry at the real center[1471] Perturbing the height[1472]

|Ak(z) − c/(z − ρ)k+1| ≤ M1/Rk.

(|c|/d) d−k ≤ (M1 + M2) R−k + C1 exp(ηU) E−k.

Since U ≤ k, the window error is at most a constant times (√(3/2)/2)k. Both tend to zero, however sparsely the integers k occur, while the residue contributes |c|/2 every time. The inequalities below apply the same comparison to the actual radii.

Choose 0 < η < log(R/d). Multiply the inequality by dk. Because U ≤ k and E ≥ R > d, the right side tends to zero along the chosen windows. The left side is a fixed positive number.

In the real-pole case take d = σ − β. At the real center the pole contributes c/dk+1 to Ak(σ) with real c > 0. Cauchy's estimate bounds the remainder by M1/Rk for R = (d + r)/2. 10Reflection and the final statement

Once every Dirichlet character has a zero-free right half-plane, the passage to classical RH is short. Two small points do most of the work. A change of modulus introduces finite Euler factors, and reflection changes the character.

10.1Removing an imprimitive level

The conductor f of χ modulo N is the least divisor through which its character on units factors. Write ψ for the primitive character at that conductor. Changing to modulus N suppresses Euler factors at primes dividing N. On the common domain of the change-of-level identity, this gives

L(s,χ) = L(s,ψ) ∏p∣N (1 − ψ(p) p−s).

For a prime dividing f, ψ(p) = 0 and the displayed factor equals one. For every other prime its absolute value before subtraction satisfies |ψ(p) p−s| ≤ p−Re s < 1 whenever Re s > 0. Each factor is therefore nonzero. The formula initially follows from Euler products and extends where the continued identity applies. The formal change-of-level lemma asks that ψ be nonprincipal or s ≠ 1. If χ is nonprincipal then ψ must be nonprincipal too, since inducing a principal character would give χ principal. Thus the exception χ = 1 and s = 1 is accounted for. From primitive to all characters[1478]

A change of modulus you can calculate. Let ψ be the character modulo 3 that takes −1 at 2. Induce it to χ modulo 6. On the odd integers the two agree, and the change removes the even terms. Thus L(s,χ) = (1 + 2−s)L(s,ψ). The factor at 3 is one because ψ(3) = 0. When Re s > 0, the added term 2−s has absolute value strictly below one. At the boundary point s = πi/log 2 it equals −1 and the finite factor vanishes. This locates precisely where the zero-transfer argument uses strict positivity of the real part.

10.2The strip theorem for characters

Assume 0 < Re s < 1 and L(s,χ) = 0. The finite factors transfer the zero to ψ. Its completed function is obtained by multiplying by the real gamma factor appropriate to the parity of ψ. The gamma arguments have positive real part in this strip, so the factors are finite and nonzero. In particular the completed function vanishes too. The functional equation for ψ−1, evaluated at s, gives a zero of the completed function for ψ−1 at 1 − s. On units the inverse character is its complex conjugate. The arguments s and 1 − s avoid 0 and 1. Returning to the uncompleted function gives L(1 − s, ψ−1) = 0.

If Re s < ½, then Re(1 − s) > ½, contradicting right-half-plane nonvanishing for the inverse primitive character. If Re s > ½, nonvanishing for χ already contradicts the original zero. This leaves Re s = ½. It proves the strip statement for arbitrary moduli. Primitive transfer, reflection and strip conclusion[1479]

Follow a hypothetical zero of a complex character

Modulo 5, the residue 2 generates the unit group. The rule ψ(2) = i therefore fixes a primitive character and ψ−1(2) = −i. If L(¼ + 2i,ψ) vanished, the completed functional equation would give a zero for ψ−1 at ¾ − 2i. The modulus is still 5. The character has changed, so the right-half-plane theorem must cover the inverse as well. Conjugating this latter zero would give a zero for ψ at ¾ + 2i. This last operation explains why the same-character symmetry in a plot is a reflection across a vertical line, even though the functional equation uses 1 − s.

10.3Why classical RH excludes the negative even integers

The public zeta theorem follows a slightly different route. Specialize right-half-plane nonvanishing to the unique character of modulus one. Suppose ζ(s) = 0 with s ≠ 1 and s outside the negative even integers. The right-hand case is impossible immediately. For Re s < ½, put w = 1 − s. Since ζ(0) = −½, s ≠ 0 and w ≠ 1. We have Re w > ½, so ζ(w) ≠ 0, and w avoids all nonpositive integers. In the normalization used by this source the functional equation reads

ζ(1−w) = 2(2π)−w Γ(w) cos(πw/2) ζ(w).

The power of 2π is nonzero and Γ has no zero for Re w > 0. If the cosine vanished, w would be an odd integer, so s would be even. Positive even integers contradict Re s < ½, zero has already been excluded, and negative even integers are exactly the excluded trivial zeros. Every factor on the right is therefore nonzero, contradicting ζ(s) = 0. This proves the implication from the nonvanishing input to the exact classical target. Classical reflection proof[1480] Modulus-one specialization[6]

Why can the same argument accommodate ζ(−2) and ζ(0)?

For s = −2 one has w = 3. The gamma and zeta factors on the right are finite and nonzero, but cos(3π/2) = 0. The equation gives ζ(−2) = 0. For s = 0 one has w = 1. Now the cosine vanishes while ζ(w) has a pole, so value-by-value multiplication at w = 1 is unavailable. Writing w = 1 + h, cos(πw/2) = −πh/2 + O(h³) and ζ(w) = 1/h + O(1). Their product tends to −π/2. The remaining multiplier tends to 2(2π)−1Γ(1) = 1/π. This recovers ζ(0) = −½.
